Từ vựng chính xác
"fully fledged language", "starting from scratch", "leave me floundering". LR: collocation và thành ngữ đúng nghĩa, không phô trương.
Lập luận mở rộng phạm vi
"Partly for the practical reason... But I think it's also about changing my own perspective." FC: đi từ lý do thực tế đến lý do cá nhân sâu hơn.
Câu trả lời một từ có nhấn
"How difficult would it be? / VERY, / I suspect." P: nhấn mạnh "Very" rồi hạ giọng ở "I suspect". Người học nên luyện cách trả lời ngắn gọn có nhấn sau câu tự hỏi.
p3samples9: Should schools teach practical life skills like cooking and managing money?

Yes, I think they should, and arguably these are some of the most neglected areas of education. A lot of young people leave school able to solve equations but with no idea how interest on a loan works or how to cook a basic meal. That gap can have real consequences, particularly with debt. The counter-argument is that the curriculum is already overcrowded and that parents should teach these things. But in practice, not every family is able to, so leaving it to the home tends to widen inequality. Even a few well-designed lessons a year could make a substantial difference.
Do you think online courses are as effective as face-to-face classes?

For some subjects and some learners, yes, and occasionally even more so. Online courses offer flexibility and let people go at their own pace, rewatching difficult parts, which suits self-motivated adults particularly well. But they tend to fall short on things that depend on interaction and feedback: practical skills, discussion-based subjects and, crucially, accountability. Completion rates for online courses are notoriously low, which suggests that many people need the structure of a class to keep going. So I'd say they're not inherently worse, but they demand more discipline, and they work best when combined with some live contact.

p2.card: Describe a book you enjoyed reading.
p2.explain: and explain why you enjoyed reading it.
p2.sample: The book I'd like to talk about is a novel I read last summer, about a lighthouse keeper on a remote island. A friend lent it to me and said I'd finish it in a weekend, and she was right. I read most of it during a long rainy weekend at home, curled up on the sofa. The story follows a man who takes a job looking after a lighthouse after returning from war. He lives alone on the island with his wife, and their only contact with the mainland is a supply boat every few months. One day a small rowing boat washes up on the shore, carrying a dead man and a baby who is still alive. Instead of reporting it, the couple decide to raise the child as their own, and the rest of the book deals with the consequences of that decision years later. I enjoyed it for a few reasons. First, the writing is beautiful. The author describes the sea, the weather and the isolation of the island so vividly that I could almost hear the wind. Second, it raises a really difficult moral question. You understand why the couple made their choice, and you feel deeply for them, but you also know it was wrong, and that tension keeps you reading. I kept changing my mind about who I sympathised with. Finally, it made me think long after I'd finished it. I ended up discussing it with the friend who lent it to me for about two hours, and we still disagree about the ending. For me, that's the sign of a really good book.
p3: Why do some people prefer reading books to watching films?
Should children be encouraged to read fiction?
Do you think printed books will disappear?
How can parents encourage their children to read more?
Is it better to read books for pleasure or for information?
p3samples: Should children be encouraged to read fiction?

Yes, I'm strongly in favour. Fiction lets children imagine life from someone else's point of view, which helps develop empathy. It also expands their vocabulary in a natural way, because stories use a much wider range of language than everyday conversation. Some parents feel that factual books are more useful, but I'd argue that the ability to concentrate on a long story is a skill that benefits children in every subject.
Do you think printed books will disappear?

I doubt it, at least not in the near future. E-books are convenient, but sales of printed books have stayed surprisingly steady. Many people like the physical experience of a paper book, and it's a relief to read without notifications popping up. Printed books also make good gifts and people like displaying them at home. I think the two formats will simply exist side by side, each suited to different situations.
p2.sample9:
The book I'd like to talk about is "Sapiens" by Yuval Noah Harari, which I read about four years ago, during a long, fairly miserable rainy season when I was going out much less than usual.

It's essentially a history of the human species, from the time when there were several different kinds of humans walking the earth, right up to the present day. But it's not a history book in the conventional sense, with dates and battles. It's much more about big ideas: how humans came to dominate the planet, why we started farming, and how things like money, religion and nations came about.

The central argument, if I've understood it correctly, is that what makes humans unique is our ability to believe in shared stories, things that don't physically exist, like money or laws or companies, but which allow millions of strangers to cooperate. I remember reading that section and actually putting the book down for a while, because it completely reframed things I'd always taken for granted. The idea that a banknote only has value because we all agree it does seems obvious once someone points it out, but I'd genuinely never thought about it that way.

Why did I enjoy it? Mainly, I think, because it made me feel as if I was seeing the world from a great height. Harari has a gift for taking enormously complex subjects and making them accessible, often with a dry sense of humour.

That said, I don't agree with everything in it. Some historians have criticised it for oversimplifying, and having read more since, I can see their point. Some of his claims are presented more confidently than the evidence really allows. But I'd still say it's one of the books that changed how I think, and these days I tend to value that more than one I agree with entirely.

"what makes humans unique is our ability to believe in shared stories". LR và FC: tóm tắt ý tưởng phức tạp bằng ngôn ngữ đơn giản, chính xác, là kỹ năng then chốt ở band 9.

"That said, I don't agree with everything in it... I can see their point." FC: thể hiện quan điểm phê phán, không chỉ khen. Đây là điểm khác biệt rõ giữa band 8 và 9.

Nhấn trong câu so sánh kết
"I tend to value THAT more than one I AGREE with entirely". P: nhấn từ chỉ đối tượng so sánh và hạ giọng cuối câu. Người học nên luyện ngữ điệu xuống ở câu kết bài.
p3samples9: Why do some people prefer reading books to watching films?

I think it's mainly about the kind of involvement each one demands. A book leaves a lot of room for imagination: you decide what the characters look and sound like, so the story feels partly your own creation. Books also give you access to a character's inner thoughts in a way film rarely can, which makes them better suited to complex, introspective stories. And reading is self-paced; you can pause, reread a line, reflect. Films, by contrast, are more immediate and often more emotionally powerful in the moment. So it's not that one is superior. They simply reward different kinds of attention.
Do you think printed books will disappear?

I doubt it, at least not in the foreseeable future. People predicted their death when e-readers first appeared, but sales of printed books have held up surprisingly well. I think that's because print offers things screens don't: no notifications, no eye strain, and the simple pleasure of owning a physical object. That said, the market will probably keep shifting. Reference books and textbooks are increasingly digital, and audiobooks are growing rapidly. So printed books might become more of a choice than a default, especially for fiction and gifts, but I can't see them disappearing.

p2.card: Describe a TV programme or online series you enjoy watching.
bullets: what it is called and what it is about
p2.explain: and explain why you enjoy watching it.
p2.sample: I'd like to talk about a cooking competition series that I've been watching for the past couple of years. It's a British programme in which a group of amateur bakers compete over about ten weeks, and each week one person is sent home. Every episode has three rounds. In the first, the bakers make something from their own recipe; in the second, they have to follow a very basic recipe for something they've often never heard of; and in the last round they create an impressive showpiece. The judges taste everything and comment on the flavour, texture and appearance. A new season comes out every autumn, and I usually watch one episode a week, on Sunday evenings, so I make it last. I mostly watch it with my mum. She doesn't speak much English, so I turn on Vietnamese subtitles and we sit with a pot of tea, guessing who is going to win. There are lots of reasons I enjoy it. The main one is that it's surprisingly gentle. Unlike many reality shows, there's no shouting or drama, and the contestants actually help each other when someone is running out of time. It's a real comfort to watch after a stressful week. I also find it quite inspiring, because the contestants are ordinary people, such as nurses, students and retired teachers, who are passionate about what they do. And of course I've learnt a lot about baking. My mum and I have even tried some of the recipes ourselves, with mixed results, I should add.

p3: Why are reality shows so popular?
Has the internet changed the way people watch television?
Should there be more educational programmes on TV?
Do you think television has a good or bad influence on children?
Will traditional TV channels survive in the future?
p3samples: Has the internet changed the way people watch television?

Enormously. People used to watch programmes at a fixed time, often together as a family, but now most of us stream shows whenever we want, on our phones or laptops. Binge-watching a whole series in one weekend has become normal. The downside is that families rarely share the same viewing experience any more, because everyone is watching something different in a separate room.
Will traditional TV channels survive in the future?

They'll probably survive, but in a smaller form. Live events like news, major sports and national celebrations still attract big audiences, because people want to watch them at the same moment. However, for dramas and entertainment, streaming services are clearly winning, particularly among younger viewers. I expect traditional channels will have to focus on live content and also offer their programmes online to stay relevant.
p2.sample9:
The programme I'd like to talk about is a cooking documentary series called "Chef's Table", which is available on a streaming platform. Each episode focuses on a single chef somewhere in the world, often someone who's quite famous in culinary circles but almost unknown to the general public.

What sets it apart from most food shows is that it isn't really about recipes. You hardly ever see step-by-step instructions. Instead, each episode tells the story of how that person came to cook the way they do: their childhood, the setbacks they faced, what they're trying to say through their food. Some of the episodes are surprisingly emotional, a chef who opened a restaurant after losing almost everything, for instance, or one who's trying to revive ingredients that her grandmother used to cook with.

I don't watch it in any regular way; it's not something I binge. I tend to save an episode for a quiet evening when I want something that's absorbing but not stressful, maybe once or twice a month. And I usually watch it with my partner, which has turned out to be a bit dangerous, because at least three episodes have ended with us booking a table somewhere we can't really afford.

So why do I enjoy it? Partly, it's simply beautiful to look at. The cinematography is gorgeous, with lots of slow-motion shots and classical music, which some people find a bit pretentious, and I can see why, but I love it. More than that, though, I think it's because it's really a series about obsession and craft. Most of the chefs have devoted their entire lives to doing one thing as well as it can possibly be done, and there's something quite inspiring about that, whatever field you're in. I often finish an episode feeling slightly more motivated to take my own work seriously.

"which some people find a bit pretentious, and I can see why, but I love it". FC: thừa nhận quan điểm khác rồi giữ quan điểm mình, thể hiện sự tự tin.
Nhấn "obsession and craft"
"it's really a series about OBSESSION and CRAFT". P: nhấn hai danh từ trừu tượng mang ý chính, ngắt nhẹ trước "about". Người học nên luyện nhấn từ khoá trong câu nêu lý do chính.
p3samples9: Has the internet changed the way people watch television?

Fundamentally, yes. The biggest shift is that viewing has become individual and on demand. Instead of a family sitting down at eight o'clock for whatever was scheduled, everyone watches what they want, when they want, often on their own device. That's given people far more choice, and it's made room for niche programmes that would never have survived on traditional channels. But something's been lost too. Fewer shows now become shared national experiences that everyone talks about the next day. And binge-watching has changed storytelling itself, with series designed to be consumed in long sessions rather than week by week.
Will traditional TV channels survive in the future?

In some form, I think they will, but their role is likely to shrink considerably. Younger audiences have largely moved to streaming and online video, and advertising revenue is following them. Where traditional channels still have a real advantage is live content: news, major sporting events and national occasions, where people want to watch at the same moment as everyone else. Public broadcasters may also survive because of their role in providing trusted information. So I'd expect them to become more specialised, focusing on live and local content, rather than disappearing altogether.

p2.card: Describe a time when you changed your mind about something.
bullets: what made you change your mind
p2.explain: and explain how you felt after changing your mind.
p2.sample:
I'd like to talk about the time I completely changed my opinion about living in a big city. When I was at secondary school in my small hometown, I was absolutely convinced that cities were noisy, polluted and unfriendly, and I told everyone that I would never move to one. My parents used to laugh at me, because they knew I'd probably have to leave home for university anyway.

And that's exactly what happened. About six years ago I got a place at a university in Ho Chi Minh City, and for the first few weeks I felt that all my fears had been confirmed. The traffic was chaotic, my room was tiny and I didn't know a single person. But gradually things started to shift. I joined a volunteering club, and through that I discovered a side of the city I hadn't expected at all. People were incredibly generous with their time, there were free exhibitions and talks almost every weekend, and I realised that the city offered opportunities that simply didn't exist back home.

I think the turning point was when my grandmother fell ill and needed treatment at a specialist hospital in the city. Because I knew my way around by then, I could take care of her, and I saw how much easier it was to get good healthcare there.

Looking back, I feel a bit embarrassed about how stubborn I was as a teenager. But I'm also quite proud that I was willing to admit I'd been wrong. It taught me that it's a mistake to judge something before you've actually experienced it.
vocab: nỗi lo của tôi đã thành sự thật
mọi thứ bắt đầu thay đổi dần
judge something before you've experienced it
đánh giá điều gì đó trước khi trải nghiệm nó
p3: Why do some people find it difficult to change their opinions?
Do you think older people are more stubborn than younger people?
What kinds of things can persuade people to change their minds?
Is it a sign of weakness when a politician changes their position?
How has social media affected the way people form their opinions?
p3samples: Why do some people find it difficult to change their opinions?

I think it's largely a question of pride. Once someone has said something publicly, backing down can feel like losing face, especially in cultures where reputation matters a lot. On top of that, our opinions are often tied to our identity, so if you challenge someone's view on, say, politics or religion, they may feel that you're attacking them personally rather than just their argument. That makes people defensive rather than open-minded.
Is it a sign of weakness when a politician changes their position?

Not necessarily. If new evidence emerges, I'd actually respect a politician more for adjusting their policy than for sticking to a plan that clearly isn't working. The problem is when the change seems to be driven purely by opinion polls rather than by principle. Voters can usually tell the difference, so I'd say what matters is whether the leader explains their reasoning honestly.
p2.sample9:
I'd like to talk about how I completely changed my mind about remote work, which is a bit embarrassing, because for years I was quite vocal about it.

Originally, I was convinced that working from home was basically a polite word for slacking off. My reasoning, if you can call it that, was that people need the structure of an office, the casual chats by the coffee machine, someone glancing over their shoulder now and then. I'd say this quite confidently at dinner parties, and I don't think anyone bothered to argue with me.

That changed about three years ago, when the company I was working for moved most of the team onto a hybrid arrangement. I went along with it rather grudgingly, to be honest. But within a couple of months, I had to admit that the evidence just didn't fit my theory. I was getting more done, not less, mainly because I wasn't losing an hour and a half a day to traffic. And the colleagues I'd assumed would disappear were, if anything, more responsive than before.

What really tipped the balance, though, wasn't the productivity side. It was noticing that my objection had never really been about work at all. It was about control. I liked being able to see people working, and I'd mistaken that for a principle.

As for how I felt afterwards, it was a slightly uncomfortable mixture. There was a bit of humility, obviously, because I'd been so sure of myself. But there was also a kind of relief, because I realised that changing your mind isn't the same as losing an argument. If anything, it's what the argument is supposed to be for. These days I try to hold my opinions a little more loosely, and I'm much quicker to ask what would actually prove me wrong.
why9: Tự nhận xét về lập luận của chính mình

'My reasoning, if you can call it that' là một chêm xen tự giễu rất tự nhiên. Cấu trúc chêm xen giữa câu cho thấy GRA linh hoạt, đồng thời giọng điệu tự nhiên như người bản xứ. Band 8 thường chỉ nói 'I thought that...'.
Collocation chính xác

'went along with it rather grudgingly', 'the evidence just didn't fit my theory', 'tipped the balance' là các collocation và idiom dùng đúng chỗ, không gượng ép. Đây là điểm LR: dùng idiom tiết chế, đúng ngữ cảnh.
Phát triển ý có chiều sâu
Phần 'it wasn't about work at all. It was about control' đưa câu chuyện từ kể sự việc sang tự phân tích động cơ. FC band 9 không chỉ trả lời đủ gạch đầu dòng mà còn có một điểm nhìn sâu, mạch lạc.
Đảo nhấn để tương phản
Khi nói 'more done, not LESS' và 'more RESPONSIVE than before', hãy nhấn mạnh vào từ tương phản. P: người học nên tập nhấn trọng âm câu vào từ mang ý đối lập thay vì nhấn đều mọi từ.
Chia cụm ý khi nói

Câu 'But there was also a kind of relief, / because I realised / that changing your mind / isn't the same as losing an argument.' nên ngắt thành từng cụm ngắn, hạ giọng ở cuối. P: chunking giúp câu dài vẫn dễ nghe.
Kết bài không học thuộc

Câu kết 'hold my opinions a little more loosely' và 'what would actually prove me wrong' trả lời phần 'how you felt' một cách cụ thể. FC: không dùng câu kết rập khuôn kiểu 'That is all I want to say'.
p3samples9: Why do some people find it difficult to change their opinions?

I think it's largely because opinions aren't just conclusions we've reached, they become part of how we see ourselves. If I've spent years telling people that something is true, admitting it isn't feels less like updating a belief and more like confessing that I've been foolish. There's also a social cost: people often hold views because their friends or family do, so changing your mind can mean distancing yourself from your group. That said, I wouldn't put it all down to pride. Some people are cautious for good reasons, because they've seen fashionable ideas come and go, and they'd rather wait for solid evidence.
How has social media affected the way people form their opinions?

It's a mixed picture, really. On the one hand, people are exposed to a far wider range of views than they were twenty years ago, which in theory should make them more open-minded. In practice, though, the platforms tend to reward whatever provokes the strongest reaction, so the views that reach us are often the most extreme versions of each side. And because algorithms keep showing us more of what we've already engaged with, it's very easy to end up in an echo chamber without realising it. I'd say the bigger change is speed: people now form opinions within minutes, often before the facts are even clear.

p2.card: Describe a skill you learned online.
bullets: where and how you learned it
how long it took you to learn
p2.explain: and explain how useful this skill has been for you.
p2.sample:
The skill I want to describe is basic video editing, which I taught myself entirely online about two years ago. At the time I was helping a friend promote her small bakery, and she wanted short clips for social media, but neither of us could afford to pay a professional.

So I started searching on YouTube for beginner tutorials. I found one channel in particular that was brilliant, because the presenter broke everything down into ten-minute lessons, such as how to cut clips, add music and adjust the colour. I'd watch a lesson in the evening, then immediately try it out on my own footage. Later I signed up for a cheap online course that came with practice files and a community forum, which was really handy whenever I got stuck.

In terms of how long it took, I'd say I could produce something decent after about a month, but it took me nearly half a year before I felt genuinely confident. The hardest part was learning the keyboard shortcuts and getting the timing right, so that the cuts matched the rhythm of the music.

As for how useful it's been, honestly it's opened quite a few doors. My friend's bakery got noticeably more customers after we started posting regularly, and since then I've edited videos for a couple of family weddings and even a small project at work. More importantly, it showed me that I'm capable of learning something technical on my own, which has given me the confidence to take on other online courses.
vocab: chia nhỏ mọi thứ ra cho dễ hiểu
p3: What are the advantages of learning online compared with learning in a classroom?
Which skills are difficult to learn online?
Why do many people start online courses but never finish them?
Should employers accept online qualifications in the same way as traditional degrees?
How might technology change education in the future?
p3samples: Why do many people start online courses but never finish them?

The main reason, I think, is the lack of accountability. In a physical class there's a teacher who notices if you're absent and classmates you don't want to fall behind. Online, nobody really cares whether you log in, so when work or family gets busy, the course is the first thing to go. Also, many courses are free or very cheap, and people tend not to value things they haven't invested much money in.
Which skills are difficult to learn online?

Anything that relies heavily on physical feedback is tricky. For example, learning to swim or to play a musical instrument properly really requires someone to watch you and correct your posture or technique in real time. Interpersonal skills are another area, like negotiating or managing a team, because you need to practise with real people and deal with unpredictable reactions, which a video simply can't replicate.
p2.sample9:
The skill I'd like to talk about is touch typing, which sounds rather unglamorous, I know, but it's probably the most useful thing I've ever picked up from the internet.

For years I typed with two fingers and a lot of looking down at the keyboard. I was reasonably quick, or so I told myself, but I always had this nagging feeling that I was wasting time. Then, during a fairly quiet stretch at work, I came across a free typing website that a colleague had recommended. It breaks everything down into tiny lessons, starting with just the home row, you know, the eight keys your fingers rest on, and gradually building up from there.

The method was simple but quite unforgiving. You weren't allowed to look at your hands, and every mistake was flagged in red. I set myself a rule of fifteen minutes a day, usually first thing in the morning with a coffee, and I stuck to it more or less religiously.

In terms of how long it took, the honest answer is longer than I expected. For the first fortnight, I was actually slower than before, which was deeply frustrating, and I came close to giving up more than once. But somewhere around the six week mark, it suddenly clicked. My hands started finding the keys on their own, and I could keep my eyes on the screen.

As for how useful it's been, I'd say it's made a surprisingly big difference. I write a lot of reports and emails, so even saving a few minutes on each one adds up. But the real benefit isn't speed. It's that typing no longer gets in the way of thinking. When I'm drafting something, the words go straight from my head onto the page, and that's made writing feel far less of a chore.
why9: Hạ thấp chủ đề một cách tự nhiên
'which sounds rather unglamorous, I know, but...' thừa nhận trước rằng chủ đề nghe đơn giản rồi lật lại. FC: cách mở bài tự tin, có giọng người nói thật, không phải mở bài học thuộc.
Từ vựng chính xác về quá trình học
'nagging feeling', 'quite unforgiving', 'stuck to it more or less religiously', 'it suddenly clicked' đều là collocation tự nhiên. LR band 9 là chọn đúng từ cho đúng sắc thái chứ không phải từ hiếm.
Thừa nhận khó khăn cụ thể
'For the first fortnight, I was actually slower than before' thêm chi tiết thật và có thời gian cụ thể. FC: câu chuyện có diễn biến (tụt rồi tiến), nghe đáng tin hơn câu chuyện chỉ toàn thuận lợi.
Câu chẻ để nhấn ý chính
'But the real benefit isn't speed. It's that typing no longer gets in the way of thinking.' dùng cấu trúc phủ định rồi khẳng định để tạo trọng tâm. GRA: dùng cấu trúc vì ý nghĩa, không phải để khoe.
Nhấn trọng âm đối lập

Nói 'the real benefit isn't SPEED. It's that typing no longer gets in the way of THINKING.' P: nhấn mạnh hai từ đối lập 'speed' và 'thinking', ngừng ngắn sau 'speed'. Người học nên bắt chước cách nhấn này.
p3samples9: Why do many people start online courses but never finish them?

I think the main reason is that nothing is really at stake. When you've paid a lot for a course and you have to turn up in person, there's external pressure to keep going. Online, especially when the course is free, it's very easy to tell yourself you'll catch up next week, and then next week never comes. There's also the isolation: no classmates to compare notes with, no teacher who notices you've gone quiet. To be fair, though, not finishing isn't always a failure. Plenty of people sign up, take the two or three modules they actually need, and quite sensibly move on.
Should employers accept online qualifications in the same way as traditional degrees?

I'd say it depends far more on the quality of the qualification than on how it was delivered. Some online programmes are run by highly respected universities and assessed just as rigorously as their campus equivalents, so it would be odd to treat them as second-rate. Others, frankly, are little more than a certificate for watching some videos. So rather than a blanket rule, I think employers should look at how the learning was assessed and whether the candidate can actually demonstrate the skill. In many fields, a portfolio or a practical test tells you far more than any certificate, online or otherwise.

p2.card: Describe a building you find interesting.
p2.explain: and explain why you find it interesting.
p2.sample:
I'd like to talk about the old central post office in Ho Chi Minh City, which is right in the heart of District 1, just across the square from the cathedral. It was built by the French at the end of the nineteenth century, and it's still one of the most striking buildings in the city.

From the outside, it has a pale yellow facade with tall arched windows and a large clock above the entrance. But what really impresses me is the interior. When you walk in, you find yourself in an enormous hall with a high, curved ceiling supported by green iron columns, and there are two huge hand-painted maps on the walls showing the region as it was over a hundred years ago. There's also a portrait of Ho Chi Minh at the far end, so it's a mixture of colonial and modern history in one space.

The interesting thing is that it isn't just a museum. It's still a working post office, so you'll see local people sending parcels and paying bills right next to tourists taking photos. There are a few stalls selling postcards and souvenirs as well.

I find it fascinating for a couple of reasons. Firstly, it shows how a building can stay useful for well over a century instead of being knocked down and replaced. And secondly, it reminds me how complicated our history is. Every time I go there, usually when friends visit from abroad, I notice some little detail I'd missed before, like the patterns on the floor tiles.
vocab: one of the most striking buildings
một trong những toà nhà nổi bật nhất
bưu điện vẫn đang hoạt động
bị đập bỏ và xây lại
p3: Should governments spend money preserving old buildings?
What makes a building attractive in your opinion?
Do you think modern cities look too similar to each other?
Who should have the final say in the design of public buildings?
How will buildings change in the future because of climate change?
p3samples: Should governments spend money preserving old buildings?

I believe they should, at least for buildings with real historical or architectural value. They give a city its character and help people feel connected to the past, and they're often a big draw for tourists, so the investment can pay for itself. That said, it isn't realistic to protect everything. Governments need clear criteria, otherwise preservation can block much-needed housing or infrastructure.
Do you think modern cities look too similar to each other?

To some extent, yes. If you look at the business districts of many Asian capitals, they're full of almost identical glass towers, shopping malls and international chains. I suppose it's because developers use the same global firms and the same cost-effective designs. It's a bit of a shame, because when you travel you want to feel you're somewhere distinctive, so I think architects should draw more on local materials and traditions.
p2.sample9:
The building I find most interesting is actually an old post office in the centre of my city. It's right next to the cathedral, so most visitors end up there sooner or later, usually by accident.

From the outside, it looks almost like a railway station from the late nineteenth century. It's painted a sort of warm, slightly faded yellow, with tall arched windows and green shutters, and there's an enormous clock above the main entrance. What really catches people off guard, though, is the inside. You walk in expecting a cramped government office, and instead you find yourself in this vast hall with a curved, vaulted ceiling held up by iron columns. At either end there are two huge painted maps, one of the city and one of the surrounding region, as they were well over a century ago.

The remarkable thing is that it's still a working post office. You can buy stamps and send parcels there, although, if I'm honest, I suspect most of the people inside at any given moment are tourists taking photos rather than locals posting letters. There are also a few small stalls selling postcards and souvenirs along the sides.

As for why I find it interesting, I think it's the tension between its past and its present. On the one hand, it's a genuine historical landmark, and the architecture tells you a lot about the period it was built in, the ambitions of the people who designed it, and who it was really meant to impress. On the other hand, it hasn't been turned into a museum behind glass. It's still doing what it was built to do, more or less, and ordinary life carries on inside it. I find that much more appealing than a perfectly preserved building that nobody actually uses.
why9: Mô tả có trình tự không gian
Đi từ 'From the outside' sang 'What really catches people off guard, though, is the inside' rồi 'At either end'. FC: bài mô tả có cấu trúc rõ mà không cần liệt kê 'Firstly, Secondly'.
Từ vựng kiến trúc vừa đủ
'arched windows', 'vaulted ceiling held up by iron columns', 'faded yellow' là từ cụ thể, chính xác, không lạm dụng thuật ngữ. LR: độ chính xác quan trọng hơn độ hiếm.
Mệnh đề quan hệ và cấu trúc đa dạng
'You walk in expecting a cramped government office, and instead you find yourself in this vast hall' kết hợp phân từ và đối lập. GRA: câu phức tự nhiên, phục vụ việc tạo hiệu ứng bất ngờ.
Rào đón tự nhiên
'if I'm honest, I suspect most of the people inside... are tourists' là hedging đúng kiểu nói. LR/GRA: band 9 biết nói giảm, nói có mức độ thay vì khẳng định tuyệt đối.
Ngắt cụm và nhấn tương phản

'On the one hand, / it's a genuine historical landmark... / On the OTHER hand, / it HASN'T been turned into a museum.' P: ngừng sau mỗi cụm mở đầu, nhấn 'other' và 'hasn't' để người nghe theo được ý đối lập.
p3samples9: Should governments spend money preserving old buildings?

Generally, yes, but I don't think it should be unconditional. Historic buildings are one of the few things a city can't simply replace, and once they're gone, a whole layer of its identity goes with them. They also bring in tourism, which partly pays for their upkeep. That said, public money is limited, and it's hard to justify spending millions on a building nobody uses while schools or hospitals are underfunded. So I'd favour preserving buildings that are genuinely significant and, wherever possible, giving them a new purpose, so that they earn their keep rather than just sitting there as monuments.
Do you think modern cities look too similar to each other?

To a large extent, yes. If you landed in the business district of almost any big city and only looked at the skyline, you'd struggle to say which country you were in. It's the same glass towers, the same chain shops, the same coffee brands. Part of that is simply economics: those designs are cheap and quick to build. But I'd add that the similarity is often only skin deep. Walk ten minutes away from the centre and you usually find older neighbourhoods, street food and local habits that are quite distinctive. The problem is that those areas are often the first to be redeveloped.

p2.card: Describe a time when you helped a stranger.
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about helping this person.
p2.sample:
I'm going to describe something that happened last rainy season, on my way home from work. It was around six in the evening, and there had been a sudden downpour, so the street near my flat was partly flooded.

As I was walking past a bus stop, I noticed an elderly man standing next to a motorbike that had obviously broken down. He was soaked, and he looked quite distressed because he kept trying to start the engine and nothing was happening. Lots of people were rushing past, probably because they just wanted to get out of the rain.

I went over and asked if he needed a hand. It turned out the water had got into the engine, and he lived about three kilometres away, which was too far to push the bike. So first I lent him my raincoat, then I helped him wheel the motorbike to a small repair shop just round the corner. The mechanic said it would take about an hour, so I bought him a hot drink from a nearby cafe and we sat and chatted while we waited. He told me he was a retired teacher and that he'd been visiting his daughter in hospital.

To be honest, it was only a small thing, but I felt really good afterwards. I think what struck me most was how grateful he was, since he kept thanking me for weeks whenever he saw me in the neighbourhood. It also made me realise how easy it is to ignore people when we're in a hurry, so now I try to pay more attention to what's going on around me.
vocab: cơn mưa như trút bất chợt
điều làm tôi ấn tượng nhất
p3: Why are some people reluctant to help strangers?
Are people in cities less helpful than people in the countryside?
Should children be taught to help others at school?
What kinds of volunteer work are common in your country?
Do you think technology makes people more or less willing to help each other?
p3samples: Why are some people reluctant to help strangers?

One reason is fear, I suppose. People worry that the situation might be a scam, or that they could get into trouble if something goes wrong. Another factor is what psychologists call the bystander effect: when lots of people are around, everyone assumes someone else will step in, so nobody does. And of course, in busy cities people are often rushing and simply don't notice that someone needs help.
Are people in cities less helpful than people in the countryside?

I'd say people in the countryside tend to be more helpful, but mainly because they know each other. In a village, if your neighbour's roof is damaged, everyone turns up to help since they've got long-term relationships. In a city you're surrounded by strangers, so the sense of obligation is weaker. That doesn't mean city people are less kind, it's just that the social ties are looser.
p2.sample9:
I'm going to talk about a time I helped an elderly tourist who'd got completely lost, which happened a couple of years ago at a busy bus station in my city.

It was early on a weekday evening, so the place was packed with commuters, and I was waiting for my bus home. I noticed this elderly man standing near the ticket booth, holding a printed map and turning it round and round, as if that might help. People were just streaming past him. I hesitated for a moment, because you're never quite sure whether someone wants to be approached, but eventually I went over and asked if he needed a hand.

It turned out he was from Japan, travelling on his own, and he didn't speak much English, let alone Vietnamese. So we ended up communicating through a mixture of gestures, my very limited Japanese and a translation app. Eventually I worked out that he was trying to get to a small guesthouse in a district on the other side of the city, and that the bus he was waiting for had stopped running on that route months ago. Instead of just pointing him in the right direction, which frankly wouldn't have been much use, I booked him a ride on my phone and waited with him until the driver arrived. I also scribbled the address in Vietnamese on a piece of paper, just in case.

As for how I felt, it was a mix of things. There was the obvious satisfaction of having been useful. But what stayed with me was how grateful he was for something so minor. It made me realise how vulnerable you can feel in a foreign city, and it reminded me of the times strangers had helped me abroad. I suppose it felt like paying back a debt, in a small way.
why9: Chi tiết hình ảnh sống động
'turning it round and round, as if that might help' vừa cụ thể vừa hài hước nhẹ. FC/LR: chi tiết nhỏ khiến câu chuyện có thật, người nghe hình dung được.
Thừa nhận do dự
'I hesitated for a moment, because you're never quite sure whether someone wants to be approached' thể hiện suy nghĩ thật. FC: band 9 kể có nội tâm, không chỉ chuỗi hành động.
Cụm 'let alone' dùng đúng
'didn't speak much English, let alone Vietnamese' là cấu trúc so sánh tăng tiến khó, dùng chính xác. GRA: cấu trúc nâng cao nhưng phục vụ nghĩa.
Mệnh đề chêm bình luận

'Instead of just pointing him in the right direction, which frankly wouldn't have been much use, I booked him a ride' dùng mệnh đề quan hệ không xác định để bình luận và giả định quá khứ 'wouldn't have been'. GRA: kết hợp nhiều cấu trúc tự nhiên trong một câu.
Nhấn trọng âm vào ý chính

'But what STAYED with me / was how GRATEFUL he was / for something so MINOR.' P: chia ba cụm, nhấn 'stayed', 'grateful', 'minor'; tương phản giữa 'grateful' và 'minor' là điểm người học nên bắt chước.
p3samples9: Why are some people reluctant to help strangers?

I think a lot of it comes down to uncertainty. When you see someone who might need help, you're not sure whether they actually do, whether they'd welcome it, or whether you might make things worse. There's also what psychologists call the bystander effect: in a crowd, everyone assumes someone else will step in, so nobody does. And in some places people have heard stories about scams or being blamed for accidents, so they're understandably wary. I don't think it's usually a lack of kindness, though. Most people, if you ask them directly for help, are surprisingly willing.
Do you think technology makes people more or less willing to help each other?

Oddly, I think it does both. On a large scale, technology has made helping far easier: you can donate to a crowdfunding campaign for a stranger on the other side of the world in about thirty seconds, and neighbourhood groups online organise help very quickly after floods or fires. But face to face, I suspect it's made us a bit less attentive. If everyone at a bus stop is staring at their phone, nobody notices the person who looks lost. So the willingness is probably still there; what technology has changed is where we direct our attention.

p2.card: Describe an app on your phone that you use often.
p2.explain: and explain why you find it useful.
p2.sample:
The app I use most often, apart from messaging apps, is a budgeting app that tracks my spending. I started using it about eighteen months ago, after I realised that I was always running out of money a few days before payday and had no idea where it was going.

It's quite simple really. Every time I spend money, I enter the amount and choose a category, like food, transport or entertainment. If I pay by card, it can actually link to my bank account and record the transaction automatically, which saves a lot of time. At the end of each week it shows me a pie chart of my spending, and I can set a monthly limit for each category. When I get close to the limit, it sends me a little warning, which is surprisingly effective.

I mainly use it in the evenings, just for a couple of minutes to check everything's been recorded properly. I also use it when I'm planning bigger purchases, for example last year I used it to save up for a new laptop.

The reason I find it so useful is that it's completely changed my attitude towards money. Before, I'd buy coffee or snacks without thinking, but when I saw that I was spending almost a fifth of my salary on takeaway drinks, I was genuinely shocked. Now I'm much more careful, and I've managed to build up a small emergency fund. So for me, it isn't just an app, it's helped me develop a much healthier habit.
vocab: dành dụm một khoản quỹ dự phòng
một thói quen lành mạnh hơn
p3: Why are some apps so popular with young people?
Do you think people spend too much time on their phones?
Should parents limit the amount of time children spend on apps?
How have apps changed the way people shop?
Is it safe to store personal information on apps?
p3samples: Do you think people spend too much time on their phones?

Generally speaking, yes. I see families at restaurants where everyone is scrolling instead of talking, and that worries me a little. Many apps are deliberately designed to be addictive, with endless feeds and notifications that pull you back in. Having said that, a lot of screen time is productive, like working, studying or keeping in touch with relatives abroad, so I think the issue is how we use phones rather than just the number of hours.
Is it safe to store personal information on apps?

It depends on the app and the company behind it. Big banks usually invest heavily in security, so I'm fairly comfortable using their apps. But there are plenty of free apps that collect far more data than they need, like your contacts or location, and sometimes sell it to advertisers. So I'd say people should read the permissions carefully and avoid giving access unless it's genuinely necessary.
p2.sample9:
The app I probably use more than any other, apart from messaging, is a budgeting app that tracks where my money goes. It's not exactly exciting, but it's changed my habits more than almost anything else on my phone.

I started using it about two years ago, after a month where I looked at my bank balance and genuinely couldn't account for where a large chunk of my salary had gone. There wasn't one big purchase; it was death by a thousand small transactions, coffees, taxis, food deliveries, that sort of thing. A friend who's much more organised than me suggested this app, so I downloaded it more or less out of embarrassment.

What I use it for is pretty straightforward. It links to my bank account and sorts every payment into categories, like food, transport, bills and so on. At the start of each month I set a limit for each category, and if I get close to it, it sends me a gentle little nudge. Once a week, usually on Sunday evenings, I spend ten minutes going through the week's spending and correcting anything it's put in the wrong place.

As for why I find it useful, the obvious answer is that I save more, which is true. But I think the deeper reason is that it's made the invisible visible. Before, spending was something that just sort of happened to me. Now I can see patterns I'd never have noticed otherwise, like the fact that I order far more takeaway food when I'm stressed at work. That's been quite revealing, actually, not just financially but in terms of understanding my own behaviour. So, in a funny way, a money app has ended up teaching me more about myself than about money.
why9: Idiom dùng đúng lúc
'death by a thousand small transactions' biến tấu idiom 'death by a thousand cuts' một cách sáng tạo, chỉ dùng một lần. LR: idiom có chủ đích, không rải dày đặc.
Lý do bắt đầu cụ thể
'couldn't account for where a large chunk of my salary had gone' dùng quá khứ hoàn thành và phrasal verb 'account for' chính xác. GRA/LR: thì động từ đúng trình tự thời gian.
Từ vựng mềm, tự nhiên

'a gentle little nudge', 'more or less out of embarrassment', 'something that just sort of happened to me' là ngôn ngữ nói thật. LR: band 9 dùng cả từ thông dụng một cách tinh tế, không cố dùng từ học thuật trong Part 2.
Ý giải thích hai tầng
'the obvious answer is that I save more... But I think the deeper reason is...' đi từ lý do bề mặt sang lý do sâu. FC: phát triển ý theo chiều sâu, có kết luận tự nhiên ở cuối.
Nhấn tương phản trong câu kết
'teaching me more about MYSELF / than about MONEY.' P: nhấn hai danh từ đối lập, hạ giọng ở cuối câu. Người học nên ngắt trước 'than' để tạo hiệu ứng.
Chunking câu dài
'Now I can see patterns / I'd never have noticed otherwise, / like the fact that / I order far more takeaway food / when I'm stressed at work.' P: chia cụm theo ý, không ngắt giữa động từ và tân ngữ.
p3samples9: Do you think people spend too much time on their phones?

Many people do, myself included at times, but I'd be careful about treating screen time as the problem in itself. A lot of what people do on their phones, like reading, studying, or keeping in touch with family abroad, is perfectly worthwhile. The real issue is the kind of use that's compulsive rather than chosen, the endless scrolling you do without really wanting to. Apps are deliberately designed to keep us hooked, so it's not simply a question of willpower. I think the healthier question to ask isn't how many hours you spend, but whether you feel better or worse afterwards.
Is it safe to store personal information on apps?

It's never completely safe, but then neither is keeping documents in a drawer at home. The risk really depends on who you're trusting with the data. A well-established bank with strict regulation is likely to protect your information far better than a free app made by a company you've never heard of, whose business model may well be selling that data on. So I think the sensible approach is to be selective: share sensitive details only where it's genuinely necessary, use strong passwords and two-step verification, and read, or at least skim, what you're agreeing to. Most breaches happen through carelessness rather than sophisticated attacks.

p2.card: Describe a piece of good advice you received.
p2.explain: and explain how this advice has helped you.
p2.sample:
The best piece of advice I've ever been given came from my first manager, when I'd just started working at a small marketing company. I was about twenty-two and very eager to impress, so I said yes to absolutely every task anyone gave me.

After about three months, I was completely exhausted. I was staying late almost every night, and the quality of my work was actually getting worse because I was rushing everything. One afternoon my manager called me into her office. I assumed I was in trouble, but instead she asked me how many projects I was working on. When I told her, she just smiled and said, "If everything is a priority, then nothing is a priority." She explained that being reliable doesn't mean doing everything; it means doing the important things well and being honest when you can't take on more.

She then showed me a really practical method. Every Monday morning, I should list all my tasks and pick the three that would make the biggest difference that week. Anything else, I could either postpone, hand over to someone, or politely decline.

At first it felt uncomfortable to say no to colleagues, but the results were obvious within a few weeks. I was leaving on time, my work was more accurate, and ironically people started trusting me with more interesting projects. Even now, years later, I still do that Monday list. I think the advice was valuable not just for work but for life in general, because it taught me that protecting my time and energy isn't selfish, it's sensible.
vocab: háo hức muốn gây ấn tượng
gặp rắc rối, bị khiển trách
từ chối một cách lịch sự
p3: Who do young people usually go to for advice in your country?
Is advice from older people still relevant today?
Why do some people ignore good advice?
Should people pay for professional advice, such as from a financial adviser?
Is it better to get advice from friends or from experts?
p3samples: Is advice from older people still relevant today?

Some of it is and some of it isn't. When it comes to technology or the job market, older people's advice can be a bit outdated, since things have changed so quickly. But advice about relationships, patience or handling difficult times is pretty timeless. My grandparents lived through very hard periods, so when they talk about resilience, I think it's worth listening to even if the world looks different now.
Is it better to get advice from friends or from experts?

I think it depends on the kind of problem. For technical issues, like a legal question or a health concern, you obviously need an expert, because friends might give well-meaning but inaccurate advice. For personal decisions, though, friends are often better, because they know your personality and circumstances. Ideally you'd combine both: get the facts from a professional and then talk it through with people who know you well.
p2.sample9:
The best piece of advice I've ever been given came from my first manager, a rather quiet woman who'd been in the industry for decades. I was about twenty-three at the time and had only been in the job for a few months.

The context was that I'd made a fairly serious mistake on a report that went to a client. I'd copied some figures from the wrong spreadsheet, and the client noticed before we did. I was mortified, and my instinct was to write a long, apologetic email explaining exactly how it had happened and why it wasn't entirely my fault. I drafted it, showed it to her, and she read it in silence. Then she said, very calmly, "Nobody needs to know why. They need to know what you've done to fix it."

At the time it stung a little, because I thought my explanation was perfectly reasonable. But she was right. What I'd written was really about protecting my own reputation, not about solving the client's problem. So I rewrote the email in about four lines: here's the error, here are the correct figures, and here's the check we've added so that it won't happen again. The client replied within ten minutes, thanking us, and that was the end of it.

As for how it's helped me, I'd say it's shaped the way I handle almost any setback, not just at work. When something goes wrong, my first impulse is still to justify myself, but I've learnt to put that aside and ask what the other person actually needs from me. It sounds obvious, but it's saved me a great deal of time and, I suspect, quite a few relationships. And on the rare occasions I've had to manage people myself, I've found myself passing on exactly the same advice.
why9: Dẫn lời trực tiếp ngắn gọn
Trích nguyên câu của người quản lý 'Nobody needs to know why. They need to know what you've done to fix it.' FC: tạo điểm nhấn cho câu chuyện, người nghe nhớ ngay lời khuyên là gì.
Từ chỉ cảm xúc chính xác
'I was mortified', 'it stung a little' là từ chọn rất chuẩn sắc thái (xấu hổ tột độ, hơi đau lòng). LR: thay vì 'very embarrassed' hay 'a bit sad'.
Tự phân tích động cơ
'What I'd written was really about protecting my own reputation, not about solving the client's problem.' dùng câu chẻ với 'What'. GRA: cấu trúc nhấn mạnh dùng tự nhiên để rút ra bài học.
Liệt kê ba ý gọn gàng
'here's the error, here are the correct figures, and here's the check we've added' là liệt kê ba vế song song. FC/GRA: cách tóm tắt nhịp nhàng, dễ nghe.
Ngữ điệu liệt kê
Khi nói ba vế 'here's the ERROR, / here are the correct FIGURES, / and here's the CHECK we've added', lên giọng ở hai vế đầu và xuống giọng ở vế cuối. P: người học nên tập ngữ điệu liệt kê này.
p3samples9: Why do some people ignore good advice?

Often it's not because they think the advice is wrong, but because following it would mean admitting something uncomfortable, that they've made a mistake, or that they need to change a habit they rather enjoy. Timing matters too. Advice tends to land when someone is already half ready to hear it; offered too early, it just sounds like criticism. And sometimes, to be fair, people ignore advice because the person giving it doesn't really understand their situation. Good advice in general can still be bad advice for a particular person, so a bit of scepticism isn't always a bad thing.
Is it better to get advice from friends or from experts?

I think they're good for quite different things. An expert, say a lawyer or a doctor, knows the field and can tell you what your options actually are, which friends usually can't. But experts don't know you, your priorities or your history, and that's precisely what friends bring. They're also more likely to tell you something you don't want to hear, provided they're honest friends. So for a technical question I'd go to an expert every time, but for a decision that's really about values, like whether to change career, I'd want both, and I'd probably weigh my friends' views more heavily.

p2.card: Describe a noisy place you have been to.
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about the noise.
p2.sample:
One of the noisiest places I've ever been to is a wholesale market in my city, which I visited early one morning last year. A friend of mine runs a small restaurant, and she invited me to come along while she bought fresh vegetables and seafood for the week.

We got there at around four in the morning, and I was amazed by how lively it was. There were hundreds of trucks unloading crates, motorbikes weaving in and out with enormous loads, and traders shouting prices at the top of their voices. On top of that, there was the constant sound of ice being crushed for the fish stalls, and loudspeakers playing announcements. It was so loud that my friend and I had to stand very close just to hear each other.

My job was mostly to follow her around and help carry the bags. I watched her bargain with the sellers, which was quite an art in itself, because she would pretend to walk away, and then they'd call her back with a better price. We also stopped at a tiny stall for a bowl of noodles before heading back.

As for how I felt about the noise, it was overwhelming at first, and I actually got a slight headache after about an hour. But after a while I started to appreciate it, because the noise was really a sign of how hard-working everyone was. It gave the place a real energy that you don't feel in a quiet supermarket. Still, I was very relieved to get home and enjoy a bit of peace and quiet afterwards.
vocab: chợ đầu mối, chợ bán sỉ
at the top of their voices
choáng ngợp, quá sức chịu đựng
p3: What are the main sources of noise in cities today?
How does noise pollution affect people's health?
Should there be stricter laws about noise in residential areas?
Why do some people prefer noisy places to quiet ones?
How can city planners make urban areas quieter?
p3samples: How does noise pollution affect people's health?

The most obvious effect is on sleep. If you live next to a busy road or a construction site, it's hard to get proper rest, and over time that can lead to stress, poor concentration and even heart problems, according to some studies I've read. Children in noisy schools also seem to struggle more with reading, because they find it harder to focus. So it's a more serious issue than many people realise.
How can city planners make urban areas quieter?

There are quite a few practical measures. Planting trees and building green barriers along major roads can absorb a surprising amount of sound. Planners can also keep industrial zones away from housing and encourage electric buses, which are far quieter than diesel ones. Another idea is to create car-free streets in the centre, which not only reduces noise but also makes the area more pleasant for pedestrians.
p2.sample9:
The noisiest place I've ever been to is probably a wholesale fish market on the coast near where my grandparents live. I went there with my uncle a few years ago, at around four in the morning, which is when it's at its busiest.

The first thing that hits you is the sheer volume. Boats are coming in and unloading, people are shouting prices across the hall, there are engines running, crates being dragged along the concrete and ice being shovelled out of trucks. On top of all that, there's a constant hiss of water from hoses, because they're washing the floor down more or less continuously. You can't have a conversation at a normal volume; you either shout or you just point.

My uncle runs a small restaurant, so he goes there a couple of times a week to buy seafood. My job, in theory, was to help him carry things, but in practice I mostly stood around trying not to get in anyone's way. He, on the other hand, was completely in his element. He'd move from one stall to the next, haggling, checking the fish, joking with sellers he's known for twenty years, and somehow he could hear everything perfectly.

As for how I felt about the noise, I was quite overwhelmed at first. After about half an hour, though, I realised it wasn't chaotic at all; it had a kind of rhythm and logic to it, and every shout actually meant something. That changed how I experienced it. It stopped feeling like noise and started feeling more like a language I didn't speak. By the time we left, as the sun was coming up, I was exhausted, my ears were ringing, but I'd genuinely enjoyed it. It's not somewhere I'd want to spend every day, but I wouldn't have missed it.
why9: Liệt kê âm thanh sinh động

'Boats are coming in and unloading, people are shouting prices..., crates being dragged..., ice being shovelled' dùng hiện tại tiếp diễn và bị động rút gọn. GRA/LR: tạo hình ảnh âm thanh dồn dập, cấu trúc đa dạng.
Idiom vừa phải
'completely in his element', 'my ears were ringing' là idiom thông dụng, dùng đúng chỗ. LR: hai idiom trong cả bài là vừa đủ, không lạm dụng.
Đối lập 'in theory' và 'in practice'
'My job, in theory, was to help him..., but in practice I mostly stood around' tạo sự hài hước tự nhiên. FC: dùng cặp liên kết có nghĩa thay vì 'However' máy móc.
Sự thay đổi trong cảm nhận

'It stopped feeling like noise and started feeling more like a language I didn't speak.' Ý ví von này cho thấy suy nghĩ sâu. FC/LR: phần 'explain how you felt' được phát triển thành một nhận thức mới.
Nhấn đối lập khi nói
'It stopped feeling like NOISE / and started feeling more like a LANGUAGE I didn't speak.' P: nhấn 'noise' và 'language', ngắt nhẹ ở giữa. Người học nên chú ý không nhấn vào 'feeling' lặp lại.
p3samples9: How does noise pollution affect people's health?

The most obvious effect is on sleep. Even if people don't fully wake up, constant traffic or construction at night disturbs the quality of their sleep, and over time that feeds into stress, poor concentration and, according to a fair amount of research, higher blood pressure. There's also the less visible effect of never having any real quiet. People who live and work in noisy environments often feel on edge without quite knowing why. And for children, persistent noise near schools can make it harder to concentrate and learn. So it's easy to dismiss noise as a mere nuisance, but the cumulative effect is quite serious.
How can city planners make urban areas quieter?

There are quite a few practical options. Traffic is usually the biggest source, so lowering speed limits, encouraging electric buses and motorbikes, and moving heavy lorries away from residential streets can make a noticeable difference. Planners can also use design: rows of trees, green walls and buildings positioned as barriers can absorb a surprising amount of sound. Then there's zoning, keeping nightlife and industry away from areas where people sleep. I'd add, though, that a city that's completely quiet would probably feel lifeless. The aim should be to protect people's homes and sleep rather than to silence the street altogether.

p2.card: Describe a family tradition that is important to you.
p2.explain: and explain why this tradition is important to you.
p2.sample:
A tradition that means a lot to me is the way my family marks my great-grandmother's death anniversary every year. In Vietnam, we call this a gio, and for my family it's almost as important as the Lunar New Year.

It takes place on the same day of the lunar calendar every year, usually some time in autumn. Wherever we are, all the relatives try to come back to my grandparents' house in the countryside, so it's one of the few occasions when three or even four generations are under one roof.

The preparation starts the day before. The women in the family, and these days some of the men as well, spend hours cooking traditional dishes, like sticky rice, boiled chicken and spring rolls. The children help to clean the house and arrange flowers and fruit on the ancestral altar. On the day itself, my grandfather lights incense and says a few words to remember her, then everyone takes turns to bow in front of the altar. After that, we all sit down together for a huge meal, which usually goes on for hours with a lot of laughing and storytelling.

The reason it's so important to me is that it keeps the family connected. I never met my great-grandmother, but through the stories my relatives share each year, I feel as if I know her. It also reminds me where I come from. My cousins and I are scattered across different cities now, so without this tradition, I think we would gradually drift apart.
vocab: sống rải rác ở nhiều nơi
p3: Why are traditions important for society?
Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?
How have family traditions changed in your country?
Should traditional festivals become public holidays?
Can globalisation threaten local traditions?
p3samples: Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?

I wouldn't say they're less interested, but they often take part in a different way. For instance, young people might not spend days cooking traditional food, but they'll happily share photos of the festival online or join a modern version of it. Busy work schedules and living far from home also make it harder for them. So the interest is there, it's just being expressed in a more flexible form.
Can globalisation threaten local traditions?

It certainly can. When global brands and foreign holidays like Halloween or Valentine's Day become heavily commercialised, they can overshadow local festivals, especially among children. On the other hand, globalisation can also help traditions survive, because tourists become interested in them and communities realise their cultural value. The key, I think, is for schools and families to keep explaining the meaning behind local customs, not just the activities.
p2.sample9:
A family tradition that matters a lot to me is something we do every Lunar New Year, on the first morning of the year. We call it 'giving the first words', and as far as I know, it's fairly specific to my family rather than a national custom.

What happens is this. Very early on the first day, before anyone's had breakfast, the whole family gathers in my grandparents' living room. Starting with the youngest, each person goes up to the eldest members of the family and says a few words, not just the usual wishes for health and prosperity, but something personal about the past year, something they're grateful for, or something they'd like to do better. Then my grandfather replies with a few words of his own, and he gives each of us a small red envelope.

When I was little, I found it excruciating, to be honest. You had to stand up in front of all your aunts and uncles and say something meaningful, and I used to rehearse it for days. But as I've got older, my feelings about it have completely changed.

I think it's important to me for two reasons. The first is that it's one of the very few moments in the year when we actually say things to each other that we'd normally leave unsaid. Our family isn't especially demonstrative, so having a ritual that makes it acceptable to be sincere is quite precious. The second reason is more bittersweet. My grandmother passed away a few years ago, and the year after, when it came to the part where she would normally have spoken, there was this long silence. Nobody planned it, but we've kept that pause ever since. So the tradition has become a way of remembering her as well, and I think that's given it even more weight.
why9: Giải thích phong tục bằng 'What happens is this.'
Câu ngắn dẫn vào phần mô tả, rất tự nhiên trong văn nói. FC: tín hiệu chuyển ý rõ ràng, không cần 'Now I will talk about...'.
Từ vựng cảm xúc tinh tế
'excruciating', 'demonstrative', 'bittersweet', 'precious' chọn đúng sắc thái. LR: 'not especially demonstrative' (không hay thể hiện tình cảm) là cách nói C2 mà vẫn tự nhiên.
Đổi thì theo dòng thời gian

'When I was little, I found it...', 'I used to rehearse', 'as I've got older, my feelings... have completely changed' kết hợp quá khứ, 'used to' và hiện tại hoàn thành. GRA: thì dùng chính xác để chỉ sự thay đổi.
Phần giải thích có hai lý do khác nhau về chất
Lý do một là sự chân thành, lý do hai là ký ức về bà. FC: hai lý do không lặp ý, lý do sau cảm xúc hơn và tạo kết bài có sức nặng.
Ngắt nhịp tạo cảm xúc

'and the year after, / when it came to the part / where she would normally have spoken, / there was this long SILENCE.' P: chậm lại, ngắt từng cụm, hạ giọng ở 'silence'. Đây là cách dùng nhịp điệu để truyền cảm xúc mà người học nên bắt chước.
p3samples9: Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?

In some ways, yes, but I think it's more that they relate to traditions differently. Young people are often less interested in the formal, ritual side, the strict rules about what you must wear or the exact order of things, especially if nobody can explain why it's done that way. But they're often very keen on the parts that feel meaningful, like family gatherings or traditional food, and many of them are actively reviving crafts or music their parents had abandoned. So rather than losing interest, I'd say they're being more selective, keeping what still resonates and quietly dropping what doesn't.
Can globalisation threaten local traditions?

It certainly can, particularly when it comes with a lot of commercial pressure. If a global festival like Halloween arrives backed by heavy marketing, it can crowd out local celebrations, especially among children. And traditional crafts often struggle to compete with cheap mass-produced goods. That said, I don't think the relationship is purely destructive. Globalisation also creates an international audience for local culture, so traditional food, music or clothing can find new fans abroad, which sometimes renews interest at home. In the end, I think traditions survive when communities actively choose to keep them, not because they're shielded from outside influence.

p2.card: Describe a plan you made that you had to cancel.
bullets: why you had to cancel it
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about cancelling it.
p2.sample:
I'm going to talk about a camping trip that my university friends and I had planned for months but ended up cancelling at the last minute. It was supposed to be a three-day trip to a national park in the Central Highlands, and there were six of us involved.

We'd organised everything really carefully. One friend had booked a campsite and a local guide, someone else had borrowed tents and sleeping bags, and I was in charge of transport, so I'd reserved seats on an overnight coach. We even had a group chat where we shared a detailed packing list and a menu for each day. Since we'd all started full-time jobs, it was quite difficult to find dates that suited everyone, so we were really looking forward to it.

Unfortunately, about two days before we were due to leave, a big tropical storm was forecast for the region. At first we hoped it would change direction, but then the park authorities announced that the trails would be closed for safety reasons. So, very reluctantly, we decided to call it off. Luckily, the coach company gave us a partial refund, though we lost the deposit for the guide.

I was genuinely disappointed, because I'd been counting down the days. But I also knew it was the right decision, as heavy rain in the mountains can cause landslides. To make up for it, we spent that weekend together in the city instead, cooking the camping food on a friend's balcony, which turned out to be surprisingly fun. And we've already rescheduled the trip for next spring.
p3: Why do people often fail to stick to their plans?
Is it better to plan everything in advance or to be spontaneous?
How do people in your country usually plan holidays?
What kinds of events are most often cancelled because of the weather?
Do you think people today plan their lives further ahead than in the past?
p3samples: Is it better to plan everything in advance or to be spontaneous?

I think a balance is best. For important things like travel during a busy holiday season, planning ahead is essential, otherwise flights get expensive or fully booked. But if you plan every hour of a trip, you lose the chance to discover things by accident, which is often the most memorable part. So I usually book the essentials and leave some free time to see what happens.
Do you think people today plan their lives further ahead than in the past?

In some ways yes, and in others no. People now plan their careers and finances more carefully, for example saving for retirement or choosing a degree based on job prospects. But personal milestones like getting married or buying a home are often postponed and less predictable than they were for my parents' generation, partly because the economy feels less stable. So life planning has become more detailed but also more uncertain.
p2.sample9:
I'm going to talk about a trip to the mountains that I'd been planning with three old university friends, which we ended up having to cancel at the very last minute.

The idea was to spend four days trekking in the north of Vietnam, staying in homestays in small villages along the way. We'd been talking about it for literally years, the kind of trip you mention every time you meet up but never actually do. Last year, though, we finally committed. We booked the guide, sorted out the train tickets and spent weeks messaging each other about what to pack. One of my friends even bought proper hiking boots, which, given how much he usually hates walking, was a big statement.

Then, about three days before we were due to leave, a storm came in from the coast, much stronger than forecast. There were reports of landslides on the roads we'd be using, and the guide called us to say, quite firmly, that he wouldn't take anyone up until it had cleared. We considered postponing by a week, but two of us couldn't get any more time off work, so in the end we just called it off.

As for how I felt, my first reaction was frustration, mostly because it had taken us so long to get organised in the first place. I'd built it up in my head quite a lot. But once the news came out about how badly some of those areas had been hit, the disappointment felt a bit trivial, honestly. Cancelling was obviously the right decision. And in a strange way, it did us some good. Instead of drifting apart again, we've rescheduled it for next spring, and this time we've all paid the deposit, so there's no backing out.
why9: Miêu tả kế hoạch bằng chi tiết hài hước

'One of my friends even bought proper hiking boots, which, given how much he usually hates walking, was a big statement.' Mệnh đề quan hệ có chèn 'given how...' bên trong. GRA: câu nhiều tầng nhưng vẫn trôi chảy.
Phrasal verb tự nhiên
'sorted out', 'called it off', 'drifting apart', 'backing out', 'built it up in my head' đều là phrasal verb thông dụng của người bản xứ. LR: dùng đúng nghĩa, đa dạng, không lặp.
Diễn đạt chuỗi sự kiện rõ ràng
'Then, about three days before we were due to leave' và 'We considered postponing by a week, but...' tạo diễn biến logic. FC: câu chuyện có nút thắt và cách giải quyết.
Điều chỉnh cảm xúc có chừng mực
'the disappointment felt a bit trivial, honestly' cho thấy người nói tự đặt cảm xúc cá nhân vào bối cảnh lớn hơn. FC/LR: thái độ trưởng thành, giọng điệu chân thật.
Nhấn từ khi đối lập
'INSTEAD of drifting APART again, / we've RESCHEDULED it for next spring.' P: nhấn 'apart' và 'rescheduled' để làm rõ đối lập, ngắt sau mệnh đề đầu. Người học nên tập câu này với nhịp chậm.
p3samples9: Is it better to plan everything in advance or to be spontaneous?

I don't think it has to be one or the other. For anything where the stakes are high or other people depend on you, like a wedding or a big work project, careful planning is simply sensible. But planning every hour of, say, a holiday can make it feel like a checklist, and you lose the chance to stumble across something unexpected, which is often what people remember most. Personally, I like to plan the framework, where I'm staying and how I'm getting there, and leave the days themselves fairly open. That way you get the security of a plan without being imprisoned by it.
Do you think people today plan their lives further ahead than in the past?

In one sense, yes. People now have tools that let them map out finances, careers and even family planning in great detail, and there's a lot of pressure, especially on young people, to have a five-year plan. But in another sense, I'd argue the opposite. Previous generations often followed much more predictable paths: you'd stay in one job, live in one town, and your life was effectively planned for you by circumstance. Today things change so quickly that long-term plans are harder to make with any confidence. So people plan more actively, but perhaps over shorter horizons.

p2.card: Describe a sport you would like to try in the future.
bullets: what you would need to do it
p2.explain: and explain why you would like to try it.
p2.sample:
A sport I'd really love to try is rock climbing, and in particular outdoor climbing on real cliffs rather than just indoor walls.

I first became interested in it a couple of years ago when I watched a documentary about a climber who scaled an enormous granite wall in the United States without any ropes. To be honest, that looked absolutely terrifying, and it's definitely not something I'd attempt. But it made me curious, so I started following a few climbing channels online, and I learned that there are some great climbing spots in Vietnam too, especially on the limestone cliffs around Ha Long Bay and in the north.

As for what I'd need, obviously I'd have to start with proper training, probably at an indoor climbing gym, to learn the basic techniques and how to use the safety equipment. You need special shoes, a harness, a helmet and a chalk bag to keep your hands dry. And for outdoor climbing, it's essential to go with an experienced instructor who knows how to set up the ropes properly. I'd also need to work on my upper body strength, because at the moment I can barely do a single pull-up.

The main reason I want to try it is that it seems to combine physical fitness with problem-solving. Climbers talk about each route as a kind of puzzle, where you have to plan your next move carefully. I think that would be a great way to switch off from work. Also, I've always been slightly afraid of heights, so I'd like to challenge myself and hopefully overcome that fear.
vocab: thư giãn, tạm quên công việc
p3: Why do some people enjoy extreme sports?
Should dangerous sports be banned or more strictly controlled?
What can schools do to encourage children to take up sport?
Why are some sports more popular than others in your country?
Do professional athletes earn too much money?
p3samples: Why do some people enjoy extreme sports?

For many people, it's about the adrenaline rush. Doing something risky makes them feel intensely alive, which is hard to get from everyday life sitting at a desk.
