There's also a strong sense of achievement when you complete something that seemed impossible, like a difficult climb or a big wave. And I think social media plays a role as well, because dramatic photos and videos from these sports attract a lot of attention.
Should dangerous sports be banned or more strictly controlled?

I don't think banning them is the answer, because adults should be free to take risks with their own safety. However, I do support stricter regulation of the businesses that offer them. Instructors should be properly certified, equipment should be checked regularly and customers should be told clearly about the risks. That way people can still enjoy these activities, but the number of avoidable accidents would go down.
p2.sample9:
A sport I'd really like to try is free diving, which, for anyone who hasn't come across it, means diving underwater on a single breath, without any breathing equipment at all.

I first heard about it through a documentary I watched a couple of years ago about competitive free divers. What struck me wasn't so much the depths they reached, although those were frankly terrifying, but how calm they looked. You'd expect someone holding their breath for several minutes to look strained, but they seemed almost meditative. After that I started following a couple of instructors online, and the more I learnt, the more curious I became.

In terms of what I'd need, the equipment itself is fairly minimal: a mask, a long pair of fins and a wetsuit. The real requirement is training. It's not something you can just teach yourself, because the risks are serious, especially blacking out underwater. So the first step would be a proper beginner's course with a certified instructor, which usually takes two or three days and includes a lot of theory about breathing and safety. And I'd need to get considerably fitter, particularly in terms of swimming technique, which is, let's say, a work in progress.

As for why I want to try it, I think it's the mental side that appeals to me most. My job involves a lot of screens and multitasking, and I find it quite hard to switch off. Free diving seems to demand the opposite: total focus on your body and your breathing, with no distractions whatsoever. I like the idea of a sport where panicking is the worst thing you can do, and where the main skill is staying calm. I suspect it would teach me something that's useful well beyond the water.
why9: Giải thích thuật ngữ cho người nghe
'which, for anyone who hasn't come across it, means diving underwater on a single breath' là mệnh đề chêm thân thiện với người nghe. FC: định nghĩa ngay khi giới thiệu chủ đề lạ.
Cấu trúc 'not so much... but' và 'the more... the more'
'What struck me wasn't so much the depths... but how calm they looked' và 'the more I learnt, the more curious I became'. GRA: hai cấu trúc so sánh nâng cao dùng tự nhiên.
Tự giễu nhẹ nhàng
'which is, let's say, a work in progress' nói khéo về kỹ năng bơi chưa tốt. LR: dùng thành ngữ 'a work in progress' đúng ngữ cảnh, tạo giọng tự nhiên.
Liên hệ lý do với cuộc sống cá nhân
Nối lý do muốn thử với việc 'hard to switch off' trong công việc. FC: phần giải thích có logic cá nhân rõ, không chung chung kiểu 'it is exciting'.
Nhấn tương phản

'a sport where PANICKING is the worst thing you can do, / and where the main skill is staying CALM.' P: nhấn 'panicking' và 'calm' như một cặp đối lập. Người học nên ngắt sau 'do' và hạ giọng ở 'calm'.
p3samples9: Why do some people enjoy extreme sports?

Part of it is obviously the adrenaline: the rush you get from doing something risky is genuinely addictive for some people. But I think there's more to it than thrill-seeking. A lot of extreme sports demand intense concentration, and people often describe a feeling of being completely absorbed in the moment, which is quite rare in ordinary life. There's also the sense of mastery: overcoming fear and doing something you weren't sure you could do. And for some, the appeal is the setting itself, mountains, oceans, the sky. So it's less about wanting to be in danger and more about what the danger makes possible.
Should dangerous sports be banned or more strictly controlled?

I'm against banning them outright. Adults should be free to take risks with their own lives, and we already accept plenty of risky activities, like driving or even rugby, without banning them. Bans also tend to push the activity underground, which usually makes it less safe. That said, I'm quite strongly in favour of regulation where other people are involved: proper licensing for instructors, safety standards for equipment, and rules about rescue costs. It seems reasonable that commercial operators should be held accountable, and that people who knowingly ignore warnings shouldn't expect the public to pay for their rescue.

p2.card: Describe a time when you were late for something important.
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about being late.
p2.sample:
I'd like to describe the morning I was late for a job interview, which still makes me cringe when I think about it. It was about three years ago, and the interview was for a position at a logistics company that I was really keen to join.

I'd actually planned everything quite carefully. The interview was at nine, and I set off at eight, which should have given me plenty of time. The problem was that, just as I joined the main road, I discovered there had been an accident on a bridge, and the traffic came to a complete standstill. I was stuck there for nearly forty minutes, and to make matters worse, my phone battery was almost dead because I'd forgotten to charge it the night before.

I managed to send a quick message to the recruiter, apologising and explaining the situation, before my phone switched off. In the end, I arrived about twenty-five minutes late, out of breath and sweating. Fortunately, the manager was very understanding. She had seen the news about the accident, so she simply moved my interview to the end of the morning, and I got the chance to calm down first.

I felt awful at the time, mostly embarrassed, because first impressions really matter in interviews. But in a strange way, it turned out well, since I got the job, and later my manager told me she was impressed that I'd let them know in advance rather than just turning up late without warning. Since then, I always leave much earlier than necessary, and I never go to anything important without a fully charged phone.
vocab: khiến tôi thấy ngượng chín người
hụt hơi, thở không ra hơi
p3: Is punctuality important in your culture?
Why are some people always late?
Should companies allow employees to choose their own working hours?
How has technology changed the way people manage their time?
Do you think people today have less free time than in the past?
p3samples: Why are some people always late?

I think it's often because they're overly optimistic about how long things take. They assume the journey will take twenty minutes in perfect conditions, without allowing for traffic or delays. Some people also try to squeeze in one more task before leaving, like answering an email. And for a few, it might be a personality thing, they simply don't feel the same pressure about time that others do.
How has technology changed the way people manage their time?

In some ways it's made it much easier. We've got calendar apps that remind us about appointments and maps that predict exactly how long a journey will take. But technology has also become one of the biggest distractions. People intend to check one message and end up scrolling for half an hour. So I'd say the tools are better than ever, but self-discipline has become even more important.
p2.sample9:
I'd like to talk about the time I turned up late to a final interview for a job I really wanted, which, as you can imagine, is not an experience I'd care to repeat.

It was for a role at a fairly well-known design agency, and I'd already got through two earlier rounds, so this was the last step, a meeting with the two founders. The interview was at nine in the morning on the other side of the city. I'd planned everything quite carefully: I'd checked the route the night before and left a generous forty-five minutes for a journey that normally takes twenty.

What I hadn't planned for was a burst water main. About halfway there, the road was completely closed, and the traffic just stopped dead. I tried to get off the main road and find another way round, but so had everyone else, and the side streets were gridlocked too. In the end I arrived about twenty minutes late, sweating and slightly breathless.

As a result, the interview started off on the back foot. I'd phoned ahead to explain, and they were perfectly polite about it, but I could tell the schedule was tight, so we had less time than planned. I spent the first few minutes apologising and trying to compose myself, which wasn't ideal. Surprisingly, though, I did get the job, and one of the founders later told me that the way I'd handled it, calling early and staying calm, had actually counted in my favour.

As for how I felt, at the time it was sheer panic, a horrible sinking feeling. Looking back, I'm almost grateful, because it taught me something quite reassuring: people tend to judge you less on whether something goes wrong and more on how you deal with it.
why9: Thì quá khứ hoàn thành có chủ đích
'I'd already got through two earlier rounds', 'I'd checked the route', 'What I hadn't planned for was...' dùng past perfect để tạo nền trước sự cố. GRA: thì đúng để làm rõ trình tự.
Câu chẻ tạo bước ngoặt
'What I hadn't planned for was a burst water main.' đặt thông tin bất ngờ ở cuối câu. GRA/FC: cấu trúc phục vụ việc kể chuyện, tạo kịch tính.
Collocation và idiom chính xác
'stopped dead', 'gridlocked', 'on the back foot', 'counted in my favour', 'a horrible sinking feeling'. LR: tất cả dùng đúng nghĩa và đúng ngữ cảnh.
Kết luận có giá trị khái quát

'people tend to judge you less on whether something goes wrong and more on how you deal with it' rút ra một nhận xét rộng hơn trải nghiệm. FC: phần 'how you felt' đi từ cảm xúc tức thời sang suy ngẫm.
Nhấn 'less... more' khi nói
'judge you LESS on whether something goes wrong / and MORE on how you DEAL with it.' P: nhấn 'less', 'more' và 'deal', ngắt ở giữa. Người học nên bắt chước cấu trúc nhấn đối xứng này.
p3samples9: Why are some people always late?

There's rarely just one reason. For some people it's a planning problem: they consistently underestimate how long things take, so they leave at the time they should be arriving. For others, it's more about personality or priorities. They get absorbed in whatever they're doing and find it hard to stop. And occasionally, if I'm being cynical, lateness is a subtle signal of status, a way of showing that your time matters more than other people's. I'd add that culture plays a role too. In some places being fifteen minutes late is perfectly normal, so what looks like rudeness may simply be a different set of expectations.
Should companies allow employees to choose their own working hours?

Where the nature of the job allows it, I think it makes a lot of sense. People's energy peaks at different times of day, and someone with young children or a long commute can be far more productive if they're not forced into a rigid nine-to-five. It also signals trust, which tends to improve morale. However, it doesn't suit every role. A nurse, a teacher or a shop assistant obviously needs to be there at set times, and even in office jobs, a team needs some overlap to collaborate properly. So a sensible compromise is core hours when everyone is available, with flexibility around them.

p2.card: Describe a friend who is good at solving problems.
bullets: what kind of problems they solve
p2.explain: and explain why you think this person is good at solving problems.
p2.sample:
I'd like to talk about my friend Minh, who I've known since we were in the same class at high school. We actually got to know each other because we were put in the same group for a science project, and while the rest of us were arguing about what to do, he quietly drew a plan and divided up the tasks. I was impressed even then.

These days, he works as an engineer for a water company, so solving problems is basically his job. But what I really admire is how he deals with everyday problems for the people around him. For example, when my laptop crashed the night before an important deadline, he spent hours helping me recover my files. Another time, when our friend's small shop was struggling, he sat down with her and worked out a much simpler way to keep track of her stock.

I think there are a few reasons why he's so good at it. First of all, he stays remarkably calm. When most people panic, he just asks questions to understand what's actually going wrong. Secondly, he breaks big problems into smaller steps, so they seem much more manageable. And thirdly, he isn't afraid to admit when he doesn't know something. He'll happily look it up or ask someone who knows more, instead of pretending.

Honestly, I've learned a lot from him. Whenever I'm faced with something difficult now, I try to ask myself what Minh would do, which usually means slowing down, thinking logically and not letting my emotions take over.
p3: Is problem-solving a skill that can be taught?
What kinds of problems do young people face today?
Do people rely too much on the internet to solve their problems?
Is it better to solve problems alone or in a team?
Which jobs require the strongest problem-solving skills?
p3samples: Is problem-solving a skill that can be taught?

I believe it can, at least to a large extent. Some people are naturally more logical, but things like breaking a problem into parts, testing different solutions and learning from mistakes are techniques anyone can practise. Schools could do more of this through project-based learning, where students tackle real issues instead of memorising answers. That kind of experience builds confidence as well as skills.
Is it better to solve problems alone or in a team?

It really depends on the problem. For something simple or very personal, working alone is quicker and you don't need to compromise. But for complex issues, a team is usually better because people bring different knowledge and perspectives, and someone might spot a flaw you'd missed. The danger with teams is that discussions can drag on, so you need someone to keep things focused.
p2.sample9:
The person who comes to mind straight away is a friend of mine called Linh. She's an engineer by training, though these days she works in operations for a logistics company.

We met about ten years ago, when we were both volunteering for a charity that organised summer classes for children in rural areas. I was in charge of the teaching materials and she was handling transport, and within about a week it was obvious that she was the one quietly holding the whole thing together.

The problems she solves are incredibly varied. At work, it's things like a shipment stuck at a port or a warehouse running out of space. But friends come to her with all sorts: a landlord refusing to return a deposit, a broken washing machine, a difficult conversation with a parent. I've lost count of the number of times I've rung her in a mild panic and come off the phone ten minutes later with a plan.

As for why she's so good at it, I've thought about this quite a lot. Partly it's temperament. She simply doesn't seem to panic, so while everyone else is worrying about how bad things are, she's already asking what we actually know. But I think the more important thing is that she breaks problems down. She'll take something that feels overwhelming and turn it into three or four small, concrete questions, and suddenly it seems manageable. She's also unusually willing to say, 'I don't know, let's find out,' rather than pretending. And finally, she listens properly before suggesting anything, so her solutions fit the actual problem rather than the one she assumes you have. I've tried to copy her approach, with mixed results, but I'm definitely calmer than I used to be.
why9: Giới thiệu người bằng chi tiết nghề nghiệp
'She's an engineer by training, though these days she works in operations' dùng 'by training' và 'though' gọn gàng. LR/GRA: diễn đạt chính xác, tự nhiên.
Hình ảnh hóa vai trò
'she was the one quietly holding the whole thing together' cho thấy tính cách qua hành động. LR: collocation 'hold something together' dùng nghĩa bóng chính xác.
Ví dụ đa dạng và cụ thể
Liệt kê vấn đề công việc rồi vấn đề đời sống ('a landlord refusing to return a deposit, a broken washing machine'). FC: ví dụ cụ thể chứng minh luận điểm thay vì nói chung chung.
Phân tích nhiều lớp lý do
'Partly it's temperament... But I think the more important thing is... She's also... And finally...' FC: các lý do được xếp theo mức độ quan trọng, liên kết tự nhiên không máy móc.
Nhấn đối lập trong câu cuối phân tích
'so her solutions fit the ACTUAL problem / rather than the one she ASSUMES you have.' P: nhấn 'actual' và 'assumes' để thể hiện đối lập. Người học nên ngắt trước 'rather than'.
Kết bài tự giễu nhẹ
'I've tried to copy her approach, with mixed results' là cách kết khiêm tốn, hài hước. FC/LR: 'with mixed results' là cụm từ tự nhiên, cho thấy người nói làm chủ ngôn ngữ.
p3samples9: Is problem-solving a skill that can be taught?

I think a large part of it can, yes. The habits that good problem-solvers rely on, like defining the problem clearly, breaking it into smaller parts, and testing assumptions, are quite teachable, and schools that use project-based learning seem to develop them well. What's harder to teach is the temperament: staying calm under pressure, or being comfortable not knowing the answer for a while. Those tend to come from experience rather than instruction. So I'd say you can teach the method fairly easily, but the confidence to use it in a real crisis is something people mostly build by having to deal with actual problems.
Is it better to solve problems alone or in a team?

It really depends on the problem. For something complex with a lot of unknowns, a team is usually better, because different people notice different things and can challenge each other's blind spots. But teams have their own weaknesses: discussions can drag on, and people sometimes go along with the loudest voice rather than the best idea. For a problem that needs deep, focused thinking, working alone first can be more productive. In my experience, the most effective approach is a combination: people think independently first, then come together to compare ideas, which avoids everyone simply agreeing with whoever speaks first.

p2.card: Describe an old object that your family has kept for a long time.
p2.explain: and explain why your family has kept it for so long.
p2.sample:
The object I'm going to describe is an old sewing machine that has been in my family for over fifty years. It's one of those heavy black machines with gold patterns painted on the side, and it's operated by a foot pedal rather than electricity.

It originally belonged to my grandmother. She bought it second-hand in the early nineteen-seventies with money she'd saved for almost two years, and it basically became her livelihood. She used it to make clothes for neighbours and to do repairs, and with the money she earned, she was able to pay for my father and his brothers to go to school. My dad often says that machine put them through education.

These days, it's kept in the corner of my parents' living room, covered with a cloth to protect it from dust. Surprisingly, it still works perfectly. My mother uses it now and then to shorten trousers or fix curtains, and when I was a child, my grandmother taught me how to sew a straight line on it, which I found quite difficult because you have to coordinate your hands and feet.

I think the reason we've kept it for so long is that it represents my grandmother's determination and the sacrifices she made for the family. Every time I look at it, I'm reminded of how hard life was for her generation and how much we owe them. My parents have already said they'd like me to keep it one day, and I'll definitely look after it, because to me, it's far more valuable than any modern appliance.
vocab: những hy sinh bà đã làm
chúng ta mang ơn họ nhiều như thế nào
p3: Why do people keep old objects?
Do you think people today throw things away too easily?
What kinds of objects are often passed down in families in your country?
Should museums display everyday objects as well as valuable ones?
Are people becoming less attached to physical possessions because of digital technology?
p3samples: Do you think people today throw things away too easily?

Definitely. Many products are now made to be cheap rather than durable, so when something breaks, it's often cheaper to buy a new one than to repair it. Fashion is a good example, because people buy clothes, wear them a few times and then discard them. This creates a huge amount of waste. I think governments should support repair shops and require manufacturers to make spare parts available for longer.
Are people becoming less attached to physical possessions because of digital technology?

In some areas, yes. Hardly anyone keeps photo albums or CD collections now, since everything is stored on phones or in the cloud. But I'm not sure people are less attached overall. If anything, physical objects like handwritten letters or old cameras have become more special precisely because they're rare. So technology may have reduced the quantity of things we keep, but increased the sentimental value of the ones we do.
p2.sample9:
The object I want to describe is an old sewing machine that's been in my family for about sixty years. It's one of those heavy black ones with gold lettering on the side and a foot pedal, built into a small wooden table.

Originally it belonged to my great-grandmother. She bought it second-hand in the early nineteen-sixties, which, from what I've been told, was a huge expense for the family at the time. She was a dressmaker, and that machine was essentially her livelihood. She made clothes for half the neighbourhood, and later on, my grandmother learnt to sew on it as well.

These days it's kept in the corner of my parents' living room, near the window. It's not just there for decoration, though. My mother still uses it now and then to take up trousers or mend curtains, and despite its age, it works perfectly well, much more reliably, in fact, than the modern electric one she bought a few years ago and hardly ever touches.

As for why we've kept it so long, I think there are a few reasons. On a practical level, it's simply very well made; nobody's ever had a reason to replace it. But mainly, I'd say it's become a kind of family record. Almost every family story from my grandmother's generation seems to involve that machine somehow: the wedding dresses she made, the school uniforms during difficult years, the time it was carried out of the house during a flood. So it's less an object than a witness, if that doesn't sound too dramatic. Nobody has ever said this out loud, but I think we all assume it'll be passed down again, and I'd quite like to learn to use it properly before that happens.
why9: Mô tả vật thể chính xác
'heavy black ones with gold lettering on the side and a foot pedal, built into a small wooden table' dùng phân từ 'built into'. LR/GRA: chi tiết cụ thể, câu gọn.
Từ 'livelihood' đúng ngữ cảnh
'that machine was essentially her livelihood' dùng từ C1-C2 tự nhiên. LR: chọn đúng một từ thay vì nói 'it was how she earned money'.
So sánh có điều kiện
'despite its age, it works perfectly well, much more reliably, in fact, than the modern electric one...' GRA: kết hợp 'despite', so sánh hơn và mệnh đề quan hệ trong một câu tự nhiên.
Ví von có rào đón
'it's less an object than a witness, if that doesn't sound too dramatic' dùng cấu trúc 'less X than Y' và tự rào đón. LR/FC: hình ảnh mạnh nhưng giọng khiêm tốn, rất giống người bản xứ.
Liệt kê chuyện gia đình theo nhịp

'the WEDDING dresses she made, / the school UNIFORMS during difficult years, / the time it was carried out of the house during a FLOOD.' P: lên giọng ở hai cụm đầu, xuống giọng ở cụm cuối. Người học nên tập nhịp liệt kê này.
p3samples9: Do you think people today throw things away too easily?

Broadly, yes, although I don't think it's entirely people's fault. A lot of products today are designed not to last, or to be impossible to repair, so throwing them away is often the only realistic option. Repairing something can cost almost as much as replacing it. On top of that, fashion and technology change so quickly that things feel outdated long before they stop working. That said, I've noticed a definite shift among some younger people towards second-hand clothes, repair cafés and buying fewer, better things. So the habit is still widespread, but there's growing pushback against it.
Are people becoming less attached to physical possessions because of digital technology?

In some areas, clearly. Most people no longer feel any attachment to CDs or DVDs, because music and films have simply moved into streaming. Photos are similar: thousands sit on our phones, and we rarely look at any of them. But I'm not sure this means we value physical things less overall. If anything, when almost everything becomes digital, the few physical objects we keep take on more significance, a printed photo, a handwritten letter, a grandparent's watch. Vinyl records making a comeback is a good example. So I'd say we're keeping fewer things, but caring more about the ones we keep.

p2.card: Describe a podcast or radio programme that you enjoy.
bullets: what it is called and what it is about
how you found out about it
p2.explain: and explain why you enjoy it.
p2.sample:
I'd like to talk about a history podcast I've been listening to for about a year. It's presented by two British historians, and each episode focuses on one event or person from the past, anything from ancient Egypt to the space race. The episodes are usually about forty-five minutes long, and a new one comes out every week.

I found out about it quite by chance. A colleague mentioned it during a lunch break when we were chatting about a film set in the Second World War, and she said there was a brilliant series of episodes about the same period. I downloaded one that evening and I was hooked almost immediately.

I mostly listen to it while I'm commuting, since my journey to work takes about thirty minutes each way. I also put it on when I'm doing housework, like washing up or ironing, because it makes boring jobs go much faster.

There are several reasons I enjoy it so much. First, the presenters have a great chemistry. They tease each other and make jokes, so even when the topic is serious, it never feels like a dry lecture. Second, they're very good at telling history as a story, with lots of vivid details about ordinary people's lives, which helps me remember it. And finally, it's been surprisingly good for my English. Because I'm listening to natural conversation rather than scripted dialogue, I've picked up loads of useful expressions and become much more comfortable with British accents, which I used to find quite challenging.

p3: Why have podcasts become so popular?
Do you think radio will disappear in the future?
Is listening to something a good way to learn?
Should the government fund public broadcasting?

p3samples: Why have podcasts become so popular?

Mainly because they fit easily into busy lives. You can listen while you're driving, exercising or cooking, so it doesn't feel like you're giving up extra time. There's also an incredible variety, so whatever your interest, from gardening to economics, there's probably a show about it. And I think people like the informal, conversational style, which feels more personal and authentic than traditional broadcasting.
How reliable is the information people hear on podcasts?

It varies enormously. Some podcasts are produced by established news organisations or experts who check their facts carefully. But since anyone can start a podcast with just a microphone, there are also many shows where hosts present personal opinions as facts, sometimes on topics like health. So listeners need to think critically, check who's behind the show and compare what they hear with other sources.
p2.sample9:
The podcast I'd like to talk about is a weekly show about the history of everyday objects. Each episode takes something completely ordinary, like the fork, the paperclip or the zip, and traces where it came from and how it ended up the way it is.

I found out about it in a fairly roundabout way. A colleague mentioned an episode about the history of queuing during a lunch break, and I thought it sounded either brilliant or unbearably dull. I listened to it that evening, mainly out of curiosity, and ended up going back and working my way through most of the back catalogue within a month.

I mostly listen while I'm doing something with my hands but not my head: cooking, cleaning or on long walks at the weekend. The episodes are around forty minutes, which is just about the right length for a walk round the lake near where I live.

As for why I enjoy it, I think there are three things. First, the presenter is just a very good storyteller. She's clearly done a huge amount of research, but she wears it lightly, so it never feels like a lecture. Second, I like the fact that it changes the way I see the ordinary world. After an episode about traffic lights, for example, I couldn't stop noticing them for weeks. And third, and this is probably the main thing, it's a welcome break from news and opinion. So many podcasts these days are about arguing, whereas this one is just about curiosity. There's no agenda, nobody's trying to persuade me of anything, and I always come away knowing something I didn't know before. In a way, it's the audio equivalent of a really good conversation with someone who knows a lot.

'she wears it lightly' (mang kiến thức nhẹ nhàng, không khoe) là cách nói tinh tế. LR: band 9 dùng collocation ít gặp nhưng tự nhiên.
Ba lý do có thứ bậc
'First... Second... And third, and this is probably the main thing...' Ở đây đánh số không máy móc vì lý do thứ ba được nhấn là quan trọng nhất. FC: liên kết có chủ đích, không phải công thức.
Nhấn tương phản
'So many podcasts these days are about ARGUING, / whereas this one is just about CURIOSITY.' P: nhấn 'arguing' và 'curiosity', ngắt trước 'whereas'. Người học nên bắt chước nhịp này.
p3samples9: Why have podcasts become so popular?

I think the main reason is that they fit into the gaps in people's lives. You can listen while commuting, cooking or exercising, times when you can't read or watch something. There's also a sense of intimacy. A good podcast feels like being part of a conversation rather than being broadcast at, and listeners often develop quite a personal loyalty to the hosts. On top of that, the barriers to making one are very low, so there's a podcast for practically every niche interest imaginable. That variety means people can find exactly what they want, rather than settling for whatever the mainstream channels decide to offer.
How reliable is the information people hear on podcasts?

It varies enormously, which is really the problem. Some podcasts are produced by journalists or academics with proper fact-checking, and they're as reliable as any newspaper. But many are essentially one or two people sharing their opinions, with no editorial oversight at all, and because the format is so conversational and persuasive, listeners can easily mistake confidence for expertise. I'd say the sensible approach is to treat podcasts the way you'd treat a conversation with a well-read acquaintance: interesting and often informative, but worth checking before you repeat anything as fact, especially on health or finance.

p2.card: Describe a time when you had to wait for a long time.
bullets: what you did while you were waiting
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about the wait.
p2.sample:
I'm going to describe a time I had to wait for almost nine hours at an airport. It was a couple of years ago, when I was flying back from Singapore after a short work trip.

My flight was supposed to leave in the early afternoon, but when I got to the gate, there was an announcement that it had been delayed because of a technical problem with the plane. At first they said it would be about two hours, so I wasn't too worried. But then the delay kept getting longer and longer, and in the end, they had to bring in a replacement aircraft from another city, so we didn't take off until nearly midnight.

As for what I did while waiting, I tried to make the best of it. I had my laptop, so I spent a couple of hours finishing a report I'd been putting off. After that, I wandered around the terminal, which, luckily, is one of the best airports in the world for this kind of situation. There's an indoor garden, a butterfly enclosure and even a small cinema, so I explored all of that. The airline also gave us meal vouchers, so I had a nice dinner, and I ended up chatting with a couple from Australia who were on the same flight.

To be honest, I was quite frustrated at first, mostly because nobody was giving us clear information. But by the end I felt fairly relaxed. I realised there was nothing I could do to change the situation, so getting angry would only have made it worse.
vocab: tận dụng tối đa tình huống
p3: In what situations do people usually have to wait in your country?
Are people today less patient than in the past?
How can businesses reduce waiting times for customers?
Is patience an important quality for children to learn?
Why are some people willing to queue for hours for new products?
p3samples: Are people today less patient than in the past?

I think so, generally. We've become used to instant results: food delivered in twenty minutes, films streamed immediately and messages answered within seconds. So when something takes longer, like a slow website or a long queue, people get irritated very quickly. My grandparents, by contrast, were used to waiting weeks for a letter, so they seem much calmer about delays than my generation.
How can businesses reduce waiting times for customers?

Technology can help a lot. For example, banks and clinics can let people book appointments online, so they don't have to turn up and wait. Restaurants can use apps for ordering and paying. But if waiting can't be avoided, businesses should at least keep customers informed about how long it'll take, because uncertainty is often more frustrating than the wait itself.
p2.sample9:
I'm going to talk about a time I spent almost eleven hours waiting at an airport, which happened a couple of years ago on my way back from a work trip abroad.

It was a connecting flight, so I was in a transit area of an airport I'd never been to before. When I arrived, the board showed a forty-five-minute delay, which didn't seem too bad. Then it became two hours, then four, and eventually, around midnight, they announced that a technical problem meant the plane couldn't fly until a replacement part was brought in. There wasn't really an alternative, so I just had to wait for the next morning.

For the first few hours, I tried to be productive. I found a quiet corner, plugged in my laptop and caught up on emails. After that, I'll admit, my productivity went downhill quite fast. I wandered round the shops, ate a very overpriced sandwich, and watched a film I'd been meaning to see. Later on, I got talking to a woman who was waiting for the same flight. She turned out to be a retired teacher travelling to visit her grandchildren, and we ended up chatting for a couple of hours, which made the time go much faster.

As for how I felt, I went through a whole range of emotions. At first I was mainly irritated, especially because the airline wasn't giving us much information. Then I got quite anxious about missing a meeting the next day. But somewhere in the middle of the night, I sort of gave in to it. There was nothing I could do, so I stopped checking the board every five minutes. Strangely, once I'd accepted it, the wait became far more bearable, and that's something I've tried to remember since.
why9: Diễn tả sự trì hoãn tăng dần
'Then it became two hours, then four, and eventually, around midnight...' dùng tỉnh lược để tạo nhịp tăng dần. GRA/FC: cấu trúc rút gọn tự nhiên, câu chuyện có kịch tính.
Thừa nhận thật thà
'After that, I'll admit, my productivity went downhill quite fast.' dùng chêm 'I'll admit' và idiom 'went downhill'. LR: giọng điệu tự nhiên, thành thật.
Từ vựng mô tả thời gian chờ
'overpriced sandwich', 'I'd been meaning to see', 'made the time go much faster' đều là collocation đời thường đúng chuẩn. LR: chính xác và tự nhiên.
Chuỗi cảm xúc có diễn biến
'At first I was mainly irritated... Then I got quite anxious... But somewhere in the middle of the night, I sort of gave in to it.' FC: cảm xúc thay đổi theo thời gian, kết bằng một bài học.
Nhấn câu kết
'once I'd ACCEPTED it, / the wait became far more BEARABLE.' P: nhấn 'accepted' và 'bearable', ngắt sau mệnh đề phụ. Người học nên chú ý hạ giọng cuối câu thay vì lên giọng.
p3samples9: Are people today less patient than in the past?

In some respects, I think they are. We've got used to instant everything: messages arrive in seconds, food is delivered in half an hour, and films stream immediately. So when something does take time, it feels unusually frustrating. But I'd be careful about saying people are less patient in general. People today still put years into training for a career, saving for a home or learning a language, which takes enormous patience. What's probably changed is our tolerance for small, everyday delays, rather than our capacity for long-term commitment. We're impatient with a slow website, not necessarily with a five-year goal.
Why are some people willing to queue for hours for new products?

There's usually more going on than simply wanting the product. For some people it's about being first, the status of owning something before anyone else, and being able to show it off. But for many, I think the queue itself is part of the experience. There's a sense of occasion and community, standing alongside people who share your enthusiasm, and companies are very good at deliberately creating that atmosphere through limited stock. There's also a practical element. Some people queue because they intend to resell the product at a profit. So it's partly enthusiasm, partly social, and partly just business.

p2.card: Describe a street market you have visited.
bullets: what you saw and bought there
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about the market.
p2.sample:
The street market I'd like to describe is a night market in Chiang Mai, in the north of Thailand, which I visited with my sister about eighteen months ago during a short holiday.

It takes place every Sunday evening, when a long street in the old town is closed to traffic, and hundreds of stalls are set up along both sides. We went there on our second night, at around seven o'clock, just as it was getting dark, and by then it was already absolutely packed with both locals and tourists.

What struck me first was the variety of things on sale. There were handmade items like woven bags, silver jewellery and wooden carvings, as well as clothes and paintings by local artists. In the side streets and temple courtyards, there were food stalls selling everything from grilled sausages to mango sticky rice and fresh coconut ice cream. We also saw street performers, including a group of children playing traditional instruments, which was really charming.

In the end, I bought a hand-painted paper umbrella for my mother and a cotton shirt for myself, and I spent far too much on snacks. The prices were reasonable, but I tried a bit of bargaining, which the sellers seemed to expect.

Overall, I absolutely loved it. Even though it was crowded and very hot, the atmosphere was relaxed and friendly, and it felt like a genuine part of local life rather than something just for tourists. It also reminded me of the markets in my own country, but with a slightly calmer, more artistic feel.
vocab: nghệ sĩ biểu diễn đường phố
a genuine part of local life
một phần thực sự của đời sống địa phương
p3: Why do tourists like visiting local markets?
Do you think traditional markets will be replaced by supermarkets?
What are the advantages of buying food from small sellers?
Should street vendors be allowed to sell on the pavement?
How has online shopping affected small businesses?
p3samples: Do you think traditional markets will be replaced by supermarkets?

Not completely, at least not in the near future. Supermarkets are growing fast in Vietnamese cities because they're clean, air-conditioned and have fixed prices. But many people, especially older shoppers, still prefer traditional markets because the produce is fresher and they have personal relationships with the sellers. I think markets will survive, though they may need to modernise, for instance by improving hygiene and accepting digital payments.
Should street vendors be allowed to sell on the pavement?

It's a tricky balance. Street vendors are a big part of the culture and many families depend on them for their income. But when pavements are completely blocked, pedestrians are forced to walk in the road, which is dangerous. So I'd suggest licensing vendors and allowing them in specific areas or at certain times, rather than either banning them entirely or letting them occupy every space.
p2.sample9:
The street market I'd like to describe is a night market in the old quarter of a city I visited in Thailand a few years ago. It's held every Sunday evening along one long street that's closed to traffic for the occasion.

I went there on my second evening in the city, mostly because the owner of my guesthouse insisted it was the one thing I shouldn't miss. I arrived just as it was getting dark, and the stalls were still being set up, but within half an hour the whole street was absolutely packed.

What struck me first was the sheer variety. One stretch was all handicrafts: woven bags, wooden carvings, silver jewellery, hand-painted lanterns. Then you'd turn a corner and find yourself among food stalls, with people grilling skewers, frying noodles and squeezing fresh fruit juice. There were street musicians every few hundred metres, including an elderly man playing a traditional stringed instrument who drew quite a crowd. In the end I bought far more than I'd intended: a couple of scarves, a small carved elephant for my mother, and an embarrassing quantity of food, including a coconut pancake I still think about.

As for how I felt, I'd say it was a mixture of delight and mild sensory overload. It was hot, crowded and loud, and at times it was hard to move at all. But it never felt chaotic or unpleasant. What I liked most was that it wasn't just put on for tourists. There were plenty of locals there, families with small children and teenagers on dates, and you got the sense that it was a genuine part of the city's weekly life. That gave it a warmth and authenticity that a lot of tourist attractions lack, and it's probably my favourite memory of the whole trip.
why9: Mở bài nêu bối cảnh rõ
'It's held every Sunday evening along one long street that's closed to traffic for the occasion.' dùng bị động và mệnh đề quan hệ. GRA: thông tin về nơi chốn và thời gian gọn trong một câu.
Chuyển cảnh trong mô tả
'One stretch was all handicrafts... Then you'd turn a corner and find yourself among food stalls' dùng 'would' để mô tả trải nghiệm lặp lại. GRA/FC: dẫn người nghe đi qua khu chợ một cách sinh động.
Từ tự giễu đúng chỗ
'an embarrassing quantity of food' và 'a coconut pancake I still think about' thêm sự hài hước, cụ thể. LR: chọn tính từ bất ngờ nhưng chính xác.
Cụm 'sensory overload'
'a mixture of delight and mild sensory overload' là collocation C2 tự nhiên. LR: diễn tả cảm giác quá tải một cách chính xác, có mức độ ('mild').
Nhấn khi đối lập du khách và dân địa phương
'it wasn't just put on for TOURISTS. / There were plenty of LOCALS there.' P: nhấn hai từ đối lập 'tourists' và 'locals', ngắt rõ giữa hai câu. Người học nên bắt chước.
p3samples9: Do you think traditional markets will be replaced by supermarkets?

In big cities, they're certainly under pressure. Supermarkets offer air-conditioning, fixed prices, card payments and a guarantee of hygiene, which many busy people value. But I don't think traditional markets will disappear completely. They offer things supermarkets struggle to match, such as very fresh produce, the ability to bargain, and personal relationships with sellers who know what you like. They're also deeply woven into the social life of many neighbourhoods. What's more likely, I think, is that the two will coexist, with markets surviving best where they adapt a bit, perhaps by improving hygiene or accepting digital payments.
Should street vendors be allowed to sell on the pavement?

I think a total ban would be a mistake. Street vendors are a big part of what makes many cities lively, and for a lot of people, selling on the street is their only realistic source of income. That said, pavements are there for pedestrians, and when they're completely blocked, people, particularly the elderly or parents with prams, end up walking in the road, which is dangerous. So I'd favour a middle way: designated areas or times for vending, a simple licensing system, and clear rules about leaving enough space to walk. That protects both the vendors' livelihoods and the public's safety.

p2.card: Describe a person you know who has an interesting job.
p2.explain: and explain why you think their job is interesting.
p2.sample:
I'd like to talk about my cousin Lan, who works as a wildlife vet at a rescue centre for endangered animals in a national park. She's about five years older than me, and whenever our family gets together, everyone wants to hear her latest stories.

Her job involves looking after animals that have been injured or rescued from illegal trading, such as pangolins, monkeys and sometimes even bears. She examines them when they arrive, treats their injuries, and then monitors their recovery. The ultimate goal is to release as many as possible back into the wild, although some animals are too badly hurt and have to stay at the centre permanently.

She didn't follow a direct path into it. After graduating in veterinary science, she worked at an ordinary pet clinic in the city for a couple of years, treating cats and dogs. But she always felt she wanted to do something with a bigger impact, so she started volunteering at the rescue centre at weekends. When a full-time position came up, they offered it to her because she'd already proved how committed she was.

I find her job fascinating for several reasons. Firstly, every day is completely different, and she often has to work out how to treat species that very few vets have experience with. Secondly, it's genuinely meaningful work, because she's helping to protect animals that might otherwise disappear. Of course, it's not glamorous. She works long hours in hot, muddy conditions, and it can be heartbreaking when an animal doesn't survive. But she says she can't imagine doing anything else.
vocab: động vật có nguy cơ tuyệt chủng
có một vị trí tuyển dụng
p3: What jobs are considered most desirable in your country?
Is it more important to have a well-paid job or an interesting one?
Why do some people change careers later in life?
Should young people follow their passion when choosing a job?
Which jobs do you think will disappear in the future?
p3samples: Is it more important to have a well-paid job or an interesting one?

Ideally you'd have both, but if I had to choose, I'd lean towards an interesting job, as long as the salary covers your basic needs. You spend a huge portion of your life at work, and if you're bored every day, the money won't really compensate for that. That said, for people supporting a family or paying off debts, a good salary is understandably the priority, so it depends on your circumstances.
Which jobs do you think will disappear in the future?

Jobs that involve repetitive tasks are probably most at risk, things like cashiers, data entry clerks and some factory roles, because machines and artificial intelligence can do them faster and more cheaply. Even parts of jobs like translation or customer service are being automated. However, roles that require empathy, creativity or physical skill in unpredictable environments, such as nursing or plumbing, should be much harder to replace.
p2.sample9:
The person I'd like to talk about is a cousin of mine, Duc, who works as a sound designer for video games. He's in his early thirties and lives in Singapore, though he grew up in the same town as me.

His job, essentially, is to create every sound you hear in a game apart from the music. That means footsteps, doors creaking, the wind, weapons, a character breathing when they're tired, all of it. Sometimes he uses recordings from a library, but a surprising amount of it he records himself. He once told me that the sound of a monster's bones breaking in one game was actually him snapping celery in a cupboard at home.

How he got the job is quite an interesting story in itself. He originally studied computer science, and for a while he worked as a fairly ordinary software developer. But he'd always been obsessed with music and recording, so in his spare time he started adding his own sound effects to small games made by friends. He posted some of this work online, and eventually a studio got in touch to ask if he'd do some freelance work. That turned into a full-time job, and he's been there ever since.

As for why I find it interesting, part of it is just the creativity involved. It's a job where you're constantly experimenting and listening to the world in an unusual way. But what really fascinates me is that it's almost invisible work. If he does it well, players never notice it at all; they just feel that the game is convincing. I find it quite inspiring that someone can put so much care into something whose success is measured by people not noticing it. And of course, the celery story doesn't hurt either.

Câu chuyện về cần tây ('snapping celery in a cupboard') và nhắc lại ở cuối ('the celery story doesn't hurt either'). FC: tạo sự liên kết đầu cuối, rất tự nhiên.
Trình tự nghề nghiệp mạch lạc

'He originally studied... for a while he worked... so in his spare time he started... eventually a studio got in touch... That turned into a full-time job.' GRA/FC: thì và liên từ thể hiện quá trình rõ ràng.
Nhấn ý nghịch lý
'something whose SUCCESS is measured by people NOT noticing it.' P: nhấn 'success' và 'not', ngắt nhẹ trước 'is measured'. Người học nên tập nhấn từ phủ định khi nó mang ý chính.
p3samples9: Is it more important to have a well-paid job or an interesting one?

I think it depends a lot on where you are in life. If you're struggling to pay rent or supporting a family, a decent salary has to come first; it's hard to enjoy interesting work if you're constantly worried about money. But beyond a certain point, extra income seems to add less and less to people's happiness, whereas spending most of your waking hours on something that bores you takes a real toll. So ideally, I'd say people should aim for a job that pays enough to live comfortably and then prioritise interest. The trouble is, of course, that not everyone has that choice.
Should young people follow their passion when choosing a job?

I'm a bit sceptical of that advice, to be honest. It assumes young people already know what their passion is, and many don't, at least not at eighteen. It also ignores the fact that some passions are very hard to make a living from. In my experience, passion often develops from doing something well, rather than the other way round. So I'd suggest young people choose something they find reasonably interesting and have some aptitude for, then stay open to where it leads. Following curiosity and building skills tends to be more reliable than chasing a single passion from the start.

p2.card: Describe a time when you tried a food for the first time.
p2.explain: and explain how you felt about it.
p2.sample:
I'm going to describe the first time I tried durian, which, if you don't know, is a large, spiky tropical fruit that is famous for its incredibly strong smell. Some people say it smells like old socks, and it's actually banned on public transport and in many hotels in parts of Southeast Asia.

It might sound strange, since I'm Vietnamese and durian is very common here, but I'd always avoided it because of the smell. Then, about four years ago, I went on a trip to the Mekong Delta with some colleagues, and we visited a fruit orchard where the owner offered us durian that had just been picked. Everyone else in the group loved it, and they kept teasing me, saying I couldn't call myself a real southerner until I'd tried it.

So finally I gave in. The owner cut it open with a big knife, and inside there were these soft, pale yellow sections. I held my breath and took a small bite. Honestly, the texture surprised me most. It was creamy, almost like custard, and the taste was sweet with a slightly bitter, nutty flavour that's quite hard to describe.

As for how I felt, I'd say my reaction was mixed. I was proud of myself for being brave, and I could understand why people are so passionate about it. But I still couldn't get past the smell, which seemed to stay on my hands for hours. These days I'll eat a little bit if it's offered, especially in durian cakes, but I wouldn't say I'm a big fan.

p3: Why are some people unwilling to try new foods?
How has the diet of people in your country changed in recent years?
Is it important for children to try a wide variety of foods?
Do you think food is an important part of a country's identity?
Should schools teach students how to cook?
p3samples: How has the diet of people in your country changed in recent years?

Quite dramatically, especially in the cities. People used to eat mainly rice, vegetables and fish cooked at home, but now fast food, sugary drinks and imported snacks are much more common. Food delivery apps have also made it easy to eat out every day. On the positive side, there's growing interest in healthy eating, so you see more salad bars, gyms and people checking nutrition labels.
Do you think food is an important part of a country's identity?

Absolutely. Food is often the first thing people associate with a country. Think of pho for Vietnam or pasta for Italy. Traditional dishes also carry history, because they show what ingredients were available, which foreign influences arrived and how people celebrated. When people move abroad, cooking food from home is one of the main ways they keep their culture alive, so it's far more than just something to eat.
p2.sample9:
I'd like to talk about the first time I tried durian, the fruit that's famous, or rather infamous, for its smell. It's quite common in Vietnam, but for some reason I'd managed to avoid it until I was about twenty.

It happened in the Mekong Delta, during a trip with a group of university friends. We'd stopped at a fruit orchard owned by the family of one of our classmates, and her father was very proud of his durian trees. So after lunch he brought out a huge one, cut it open right in front of us, and there was really no polite way of refusing.

The first thing, of course, was the smell. People describe it in all sorts of colourful ways, and I won't repeat most of them, but it's a strong, heavy smell, a bit like onions mixed with something very sweet. I remember hesitating for quite a long time, while my friends, who'd all grown up eating it, were laughing at my expression. Eventually I took a small piece. The texture was the real surprise: it was soft and creamy, almost like custard, and the flavour was nothing like the smell. It was rich and sweet, with a slightly nutty, almost savoury undertone.

As for how I felt about it, I'd say it was a genuine shock, but a pleasant one. I wouldn't claim I fell in love with it immediately, but by the third piece I could see why people are so passionate about it. More than the fruit itself, though, it taught me something about first impressions. I'd spent years avoiding it based on a reputation, and it turned out I'd been missing out. These days I'm much more willing to try things I'm unsure about, and durian has become one of my favourite fruits, much to my friends' amusement.
why9: Tự sửa lời để chính xác
'famous, or rather infamous, for its smell' dùng 'or rather' để điều chỉnh từ. LR: phân biệt 'famous' và 'infamous' chính xác, cách tự sửa rất tự nhiên.
Mô tả mùi vị tinh tế
'soft and creamy, almost like custard', 'rich and sweet, with a slightly nutty, almost savoury undertone'. LR: từ vựng mô tả cảm quan chính xác, có mức độ ('slightly', 'almost').
Né tránh khéo léo
'People describe it in all sorts of colourful ways, and I won't repeat most of them' là cách nói hài hước, lịch sự. LR/FC: 'colourful' theo nghĩa bóng (thô tục) dùng đúng.
Từ trải nghiệm đến bài học
'More than the fruit itself, though, it taught me something about first impressions.' FC: phát triển từ chuyện ăn uống sang bài học về định kiến, câu trả lời có chiều sâu.
Nhấn tương phản mùi và vị
'the FLAVOUR was nothing like the SMELL.' P: nhấn hai danh từ đối lập, ngắt nhẹ sau 'flavour'. Người học nên tránh nhấn vào 'nothing like' mà nhấn vào hai đối tượng được so sánh.
p3samples9: Why are some people unwilling to try new foods?

Part of it is probably biological. Humans have evolved to be wary of unfamiliar foods, because historically, eating the wrong thing could make you seriously ill. But a lot of it is cultural and psychological too. If you've grown up with a fairly narrow diet, unfamiliar textures or smells can feel genuinely off-putting, and some people are anxious about looking foolish if they don't like something in front of others. Habit plays a role as well; when you're tired or busy, it's easier to stick with what you know. That said, most people become more adventurous with exposure, especially when they're with people they trust.
Do you think food is an important part of a country's identity?

Absolutely, and I'd say it's one of the most accessible parts. Food carries a lot of history: the ingredients reflect the climate and geography, and many dishes show traces of trade, migration and even colonisation. For people living abroad, it's often the thing they miss most, and cooking traditional food becomes a way of staying connected to home. That said, national cuisines are rarely as fixed or pure as people like to think. Many so-called traditional dishes were adapted from other cultures surprisingly recently. So food is central to identity, but it's an identity that's always been evolving.

p2.card: Describe a photo you took that you are proud of.
bullets: when and where you took it
p2.explain: and explain why you are proud of this photo.
p2.sample:
The photo I'm proudest of is one I took of my grandfather on the morning of his eightieth birthday. It shows him sitting on the wooden bench outside his house in the countryside, holding a cup of tea and laughing at something my little nephew had just said. The early sunlight is coming in from the side, so half of his face is lit up and you can see all the lines around his eyes.

I took it about two years ago. The whole family had gathered at his house for the celebration, and while everyone else was busy preparing food, I noticed him sitting outside on his own, looking really content.

I didn't have a professional camera, just my phone, but I'd been watching a lot of photography tutorials, so I tried to apply what I'd learned. I crouched down so that the camera was at his eye level, switched to portrait mode to blur the background, and turned off the flash so the light would look natural. I took around twenty shots, and this was the only one where he was laughing naturally rather than posing.

The reason I'm so proud of it is partly technical, because I think it's the first time I really got the light right. But mainly it's because it captures his personality perfectly, warm and full of humour. My family loved it so much that we had it printed and framed, and it now hangs in his living room. Sadly, his health has declined since then, so that photo has become even more precious to all of us.
vocab: lột tả được tính cách của ai
p3: Why do people take so many photos nowadays?
Do you think photos on social media give a true picture of people's lives?
Is photography a real art form?
Should people be allowed to take photos of strangers in public places?
How do you think people will store their memories in the future?
p3samples: Do you think photos on social media give a true picture of people's lives?

Not really. Most people only post the highlights, like holidays, parties or special meals, and many photos are carefully edited or filtered. So what you see is a very selective version of someone's life. The risk is that viewers, especially teenagers, compare their own ordinary days with these perfect images and end up feeling inadequate, even though nobody's life actually looks like that all the time.
Should people be allowed to take photos of strangers in public places?

Legally, in many countries, it's allowed, and I understand why, since street photography can record history and everyday life. But I think there's an ethical side too. If someone is clearly the main subject of the photo, it's polite to ask permission, especially before posting it online. And photographing children or people in vulnerable situations, like at a hospital, should definitely be avoided without consent.
p2.sample9:
The photo I'm most proud of is one I took of my grandfather about four years ago, sitting at the small wooden table in his kitchen, reading a newspaper by the window.

It was taken on an ordinary weekday morning when I was visiting my grandparents in the countryside. I was up early, and I wandered into the kitchen while he was having his morning tea. The light was coming in at a very low angle through the window, which had those old wooden shutters, so there were strips of light and shadow across the table and across his face. He had his glasses pushed down his nose and he was completely absorbed in the paper.

As for how I took it, there was nothing sophisticated about it, really. I just had my phone with me. What I did do was resist the temptation to ask him to pose. I stood in the doorway and took about five or six shots very quietly, and he didn't notice at all. Later on, I converted it to black and white, which I think brought out the contrast in the light, but I didn't edit it much beyond that.

The reason I'm proud of it isn't really technical. There's nothing particularly clever about the composition, and the focus is slightly soft. But it captures him exactly as he was, in a way that more formal photos never did. When people pose, they put on a slightly different face. In this one he's just himself, completely unaware of the camera. He passed away last year, and that photo has become very precious to my family. It's now framed in my grandmother's living room, and when people see it, they always say the same thing: that's exactly how he was.
why9: Mô tả ánh sáng chi tiết
'The light was coming in at a very low angle... so there were strips of light and shadow across the table and across his face.' LR/FC: mô tả cụ thể, giúp người nghe 'nhìn' thấy bức ảnh.
Nhấn mạnh bằng trợ động từ 'did'
'What I did do was resist the temptation to ask him to pose.' dùng 'did' nhấn mạnh trong câu chẻ. GRA: cấu trúc nhấn mạnh tự nhiên, đối lập với câu trước 'nothing sophisticated'.
Collocation nhiếp ảnh vừa đủ
'brought out the contrast', 'the composition', 'the focus is slightly soft'. LR: từ chuyên môn dùng đúng và không quá kỹ thuật.
Lý do tự hào không nằm ở kỹ thuật
'The reason I'm proud of it isn't really technical.' rồi giải thích ý nghĩa cảm xúc. FC: trả lời phần 'explain' bằng một góc nhìn bất ngờ, có chiều sâu.
Nhịp chậm khi kể phần cảm xúc

'He passed away last year, / and that photo has become very PRECIOUS to my family.' P: chậm lại, ngắt sau 'last year', nhấn 'precious'. Người học nên bắt chước cách dùng nhịp chậm cho câu mang cảm xúc.
p3samples9: Do you think photos on social media give a true picture of people's lives?

Not really, and I think most people know that, even if they don't always remember it while scrolling. What people post is heavily selected: the holiday, the nice meal, the good hair day, rarely the dull or difficult moments. And with filters and editing, even those moments are often polished. That doesn't make the photos lies exactly; they're real moments, just very unrepresentative ones. The risk is that people compare their ordinary, unedited lives with everyone else's highlights, which can leave them feeling inadequate. There's been a bit of a backlash recently, with people posting more casual, unfiltered content, but the basic tendency hasn't changed.
Should people be allowed to take photos of strangers in public places?

Legally, in most places, they are, and I think that's broadly right. Banning it would make street photography and even simple holiday snaps almost impossible, and some of the most valuable historical photos are of ordinary people in public. But I think there's an important difference between taking a photo and what you do with it. Posting a picture of a stranger online in order to mock them, or using it commercially without permission, is a different matter entirely. So rather than restricting the act of photography, I'd focus on respecting people's dignity, and giving them a clear way to ask for images to be removed.

p2.card: Describe a time when you received good news.
bullets: when and how you received it
p2.explain: and explain how you felt when you received the news.
p2.sample:
I'd like to describe the day I found out that I'd been awarded a scholarship for a short summer programme abroad. It was a six-week course in environmental management at a university in Australia, fully funded, including flights and accommodation.

I received the news about three years ago, in the middle of a very ordinary Tuesday. I was on my lunch break at work, scrolling through my emails, when I saw a message from the scholarship committee. I'd applied about four months earlier and had almost given up hope, because I'd heard that thousands of people applied for only a handful of places. So when I opened it, I had to read the first line three times before I really believed it said "Congratulations".

The first person I called was my mother. She was so excited that she started crying on the phone, and then she immediately rang all the relatives, so within an hour my whole extended family knew. That evening, my closest friends took me out for a celebratory dinner at a little hotpot restaurant we love.

As for how I felt, it was a mixture of emotions. Obviously I was thrilled and incredibly relieved, because I'd put a lot of effort into my application, writing and rewriting my personal statement many times. But I also felt a bit nervous, since I'd never travelled so far on my own before. Looking back, though, that experience was a real turning point. It gave me much more confidence and it's the main reason I later decided to continue studying in that field.
p3: How do people usually share good news in your country?
Why do the media focus more on bad news than good news?
Is it better to hear bad news in person or by message?
Do you think people are less excited by good news than they used to be?
Should news programmes include more positive stories?
p3samples: Why do the media focus more on bad news than good news?

Partly it's human nature. We're naturally more alert to threats, so stories about disasters, crime or conflict grab our attention more than positive ones. And because media companies depend on clicks and viewing figures, they give audiences what keeps them watching. There's also a sense that bad news is more urgent, since it may require action, whereas good news often seems less important, even when it isn't.
Is it better to hear bad news in person or by message?

For serious news, like a death or a health problem, I think it should definitely be delivered in person or at least by phone. Hearing it from someone who can comfort you makes a big difference, and a text can feel cold or be misunderstood. However, for minor disappointments, like a cancelled event, a message is fine and even preferable, because it gives the person time to react privately.
p2.sample9:
I'd like to talk about the day I found out I'd been accepted onto a master's programme abroad, with a full scholarship. It was about five years ago, and I still remember it in a lot of detail.

I'd applied about six months earlier, and the process had been long and fairly stressful: essays, references, an interview over a very unreliable video call. The results were supposed to come out at the end of March, but the date came and went with nothing. I'd more or less convinced myself that silence meant rejection.

Then, one morning in early April, I was on the bus to work, half asleep, scrolling through my emails, and there it was. The subject line just said 'Your application', which told me nothing. I remember holding my phone for a few seconds before opening it, partly out of nerves and partly because I wanted to delay finding out. When I finally read the first line, which started with 'We are delighted to inform you', I had to read it three times to make sure I hadn't misunderstood.

The first person I told was my mother. I rang her straight away, still on the bus, and probably far too loudly for a crowded bus at eight in the morning. She didn't say anything for a moment, and then she started crying, which set me off as well. After that, I messaged a couple of close friends and my former teacher who'd written one of my references.

As for how I felt, it was a mixture of elation and pure relief. But more than anything, I think it was a sense that all the effort had actually counted for something. And honestly, a part of me was quite scared too, because I suddenly realised it was real, and I'd have to move to the other side of the world.
why9: Tạo kỳ vọng và hồi hộp
'the date came and went with nothing. I'd more or less convinced myself that silence meant rejection.' FC: xây dựng căng thẳng trước khi đến tin tốt, câu chuyện có cao trào.
Cấu trúc 'there it was'
'scrolling through my emails, and there it was.' là cấu trúc đảo ngắn gọn, tạo khoảnh khắc. GRA: dùng đảo ngữ tự nhiên trong văn kể.
Lý do hành động có hai vế
'partly out of nerves and partly because I wanted to delay finding out' dùng cặp 'partly... partly'. GRA/LR: giải thích động cơ tinh tế, hai vế song song.
Từ vựng cảm xúc đa dạng
'elation and pure relief', 'which set me off as well', 'counted for something'. LR: phrasal verb 'set me off' (làm tôi khóc theo) và collocation chính xác.
Nhấn khi chuyển ý
'And HONESTLY, / a part of me was quite SCARED too.' P: ngắt sau 'honestly', nhấn 'scared' để thể hiện cảm xúc trái chiều. Người học nên tập ngắt nhịp trước ý bất ngờ.
Kết bài có cảm xúc đa chiều
Kết bằng nỗi sợ bên cạnh niềm vui: 'I'd have to move to the other side of the world.' FC: không chỉ nói 'I was very happy' mà thể hiện cảm xúc phức tạp, thật hơn.
p3samples9: Why do the media focus more on bad news than good news?

Partly it's simply human nature. We're more alert to threats than to good news, probably for evolutionary reasons, so negative stories grab our attention and get more clicks. Since many media outlets depend on attention for advertising revenue, they have a strong incentive to lead with crises, crime and conflict. There's also a more defensible reason: journalism is supposed to hold power to account, which naturally means highlighting problems. Good news is often gradual, like falling poverty rates over decades, and doesn't fit the format of breaking news. So it's a mix of commercial pressure and the nature of news itself.
Should news programmes include more positive stories?

I think so, within reason. If people are only exposed to bad news, they can end up with a distorted, overly bleak view of the world, and that can lead to apathy, a sense that nothing can be done. Including stories about problems being solved, rather than just problems, can actually make audiences more engaged. That said, positive stories shouldn't come at the expense of serious reporting, and there's a danger of them becoming trivial, heartwarming filler. What I'd like to see isn't fluffy good news, but more reporting on solutions: what's working, where and why.
